# Om! Salutations to the Illustrious Ganesha. 

# Om! May the wish-fulfilling jewel <note>original: "Cintāmaṇi"</note> who removes all obstacles be victorious—he whose splendor is like the morning sun, who is the lord of all wisdom, whose fame is celebrated by the wise, and who is served by those seeking to behold the entirety of the world's truths. (1)

Having bowed to the speech of the Guru and the elephant-faced deity <note>Lord Ganesha</note>, this commentary titled "The Teacher’s Grace for Easy Understanding" <note>original: "Gurukṛpasvarabodhika"</note> is expanded upon this excellent scripture named **The Ornament of Astrologers** <note>original: "Jyotirvidābharaṇam"</note>, which was composed by the great king of poets, **Shri Kalidasa**. (2)

In the city of Pattana <note>likely Patan in Gujarat</note>, at the gateway of the Durgahredhherapha fortress, this work was requested for the benefit of others by **Bhavamuni**, the student of the glorious and venerable King of Sages, Prabhusuri. (3)

<margin>
357 Leaves
The Astrologer
Kalidasa
</margin>

Now, at the beginning of the book, the author **Shri Kalidasa, the King of Poets**, performs the "Auspicious Invocation" <note>original: "Maṅgalācaraṇa"</note>—taking the form of a salute to his chosen deity—and describes the "Four Indispensable Elements" <note>original: "Anubandha Catuṣṭaya," referring to the subject, purpose, relationship, and the intended audience</note> using the *Vasantatilaka* meter. 

He asks: "Is it not so?"—this particle "nanu" is used to signify certainty at the start of a work. It is said that "nanu" is used for certainty, questioning, and emphasis. This poet named Kalidasa is seen in many texts and is well-known among the community of scholars <note>original: "Vipra"</note>. The practical usage and reputation of this name are established by the words of the people. This usage is systematic, starting from the sacraments of conception <note>original: "Garbhādhāna"</note> up until the time of writing this book. This is because he was favored by the goddess Saraswati. To achieve the perfect result, he addresses the community of people—either the assembly of readers or those who follow his words. This "behavior of people" or "social conduct" is established through the reading of the scriptures. This is the conduct of the common man, or rather, the conduct among scholars. For those wise people whose speech is sweet, the extension of meaning is seen in the mouth and the mind. Thus, there are many ways of explaining this. Therefore, the physical body is understood as a "vessel of wisdom" <note>original: "prakāśo"</note>. The dictionary **The Jewel of Names** <note>original: "Abhidhāna Cintāmaṇi," a famous lexicon by Hemachandra</note> defines "body" <note>original: "vapur"</note> as a collection of elements. By these names...

<margin>
Rama 1
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the introductory commentary on the "Ornament of Astrologers." The previous page concluded with the commentator, Bhavamuni, beginning to analyze the opening verse and the framework of the work. This page focuses on the specific sages who inspired the text and addresses potential phonetic concerns regarding the opening word.</meta>

That which was proclaimed, spoken, or brought into the realm of speech by the voices of the Sages—or rather, revealed as being within the reach of words—is here presented. Even if it is said by someone who possesses self-awareness of their own perspective <note>original: "svābhimāna-nayana"</note>, it is suggested that "my own intellect enters into this following the path of the original threads" <note>original: "sūtra-gativadatra mame mati-praveśaḥ"</note>. Thus, it is heard that I am composing—that is, I am explaining—this book named **The Ornament of Astrologers** <note>original: "Jyotirvidābharaṇam"</note>. By this very act, any notion that this work arises merely from the whims of my own mind is cast aside. 

The word "Jyotirvid" <note>original: "jyotir-vidaḥ"</note> refers to the "knowers of light," meaning the diviners or astrologers. This book is like an "ornament" <note>original: "ābharaṇam"</note> or a piece of jewelry for them. Alternatively, it is an ornament for the knowledge and wisdom of the science of light <note>astrology/astronomy</note>. The grammatical use of the present tense "I compose" implies an action that is starting now and continuing into the near future. Why is this done? It is for the purpose of establishing a connection...

# Om! Salutations to the Illustrious Ganesha.

## Om! That which was proclaimed by the Sages Raibhya, Atri, Harita, Vasishtha, and Parashara for the success of people’s worldly dealings.

Through the effort related to the Sun <note>the solar calendar/influence</note>, victory is found in the abode of splendor related to the Auspicious One <note>Lord Shiva</note>. Here, the phrase "victory be to" <note>original: "vijayate"</note> constitutes a verbal salutation. 

The following elements of the work's framework are thus indicated:
1. **The Subject Matter** <note>original: "viṣaya"</note>: The solar and auspicious splendor.
2. **The Purpose** <note>original: "prayojanam"</note>: Specifically, "for the success of people's worldly dealings" <note>meaning to help people manage their daily affairs through astrological timing</note>.
3. **The Intended Audience** <note>original: "adhikāriṇaḥ"</note>: Those suggested by the term "Knowers of Light" <note>Astrologers</note>.
4. **The Relationship** <note>original: "sambandhaḥ"</note>: Primarily the relationship between the "thing to be explained" (the astrological principles) and the "book that explains" (this text).

<margin>
The path of the Sages
The four-fold framework
</margin>

Now, a doubt might be raised: In the beginning of a book, does the use of the letter 'R' <note>the "repha" or 'r' sound</note> in the name **Raibhya** cause an obstacle? One might argue that the letter 'R' is harmful or inauspicious. However, this rule regarding poetic meters is set aside here because the word refers to the name of a Sage. Since it refers to an actual person or substance <note>original: "dravya-vācitvāt"</note>, this opening is considered entirely free of obstacles. 

In this commentary, "The Teacher’s Grace for Easy Understanding" <note>original: "Subodhikā"</note>, where the rules of grammar and connection...

<summary>The commentator explains the title "Ornament of Astrologers" and breaks down the work's purpose: helping people navigate life through the wisdom of ancient sages like Vasishtha and Parashara. He also defends starting the poem with the name "Raibhya," arguing that the holiness of the sage overrides any technical rules about inauspicious sounds.</summary>

<margin>
Commentary on the Ornament of Astrologers, Page 1
</margin>

Now, one might ask: if the truth was already seen and understood by the ancient sages, why is this new work necessary? Furthermore, one might argue that according to the *Hemasutra* <note>original: "haimasūtreṇa," referring to the grammar rules of Hemacandra</note>, a phonetic junction <term>sandhi|the blending of sounds at word boundaries</term> should not occur where there is a natural pause, thus suggesting an error in the opening. In this book, although I follow the path proclaimed by the poet **Kalidasa** and the great astronomer **Varahamihira**, I have also integrated the views of many grammarians to address the linguistic faults often found in the speech of diviners <note>astrologers</note>. Even if there are difficult phonetic combinations or complex words used, they are justified by the living tradition of the verse. Nevertheless, this undertaking is made strong by the grace of the illustrious **Mahima Prabha Surisvara**, a master who understands both his own traditions and the traditions of others.

In the composition of this work, I have consulted the following authoritative texts: the *Abhidhāna Cintāmaṇi* <note>Hemacandra’s famous lexicon of synonyms</note>, the *Haima Book of Many Meanings*, the *Supplementary Haima Lexicon*, the *Mahipa Lexicons*, the *Medley of Multi-Meaning Sounds*, various *Single-Syllable Lexicons*, the *Ocean of Word-Jewels*, the *Distinction of Words*, the *Haima Instruction on Gender*, the *Great Commentary on Hemacandra*, and the *Ocean of Verbs*. I have followed these sources according to my own limited intellect. Therefore, the wise should not be confused by my method, but should instead set aside all malice and correct any errors they find.

-> I begin this book; indeed, it is the very speech which is a great ornament for the knowers of the lights <note>astrologers</note>. 1. <-

### On the Distinction of Words

Now, for the sake of clarity of intellect, some distinctions regarding the gender and usage of words are recorded. The terms *Ashvi*, *Ashvahasta*, *Shravana*, *Tithita*, and *Shravasthi* are either masculine or feminine. The word *Taraka* <note>star</note> can be used in all three genders <note>masculine, feminine, or neuter</note>. *Udu* <note>lunar mansion</note> is feminine or neuter. *Asayuk* is feminine. *Mrigashira* is masculine or neuter. *Shatabhishak* is feminine. In the science of astrology, the names of the months are typically neuter. The word *Punarvasu* <note>a specific Nakshatra or star cluster</note> is used in the dual masculine. *Magha* and *Krittika* are always used in the feminine plural. 

Regarding time, for the terms *Ahne* <note>day</note>, *Hayana* <note>year</note>, *Varsha* <note>year</note>, and *Marute* <note>day/wind</note>, one may use *Dina*, *Divasa*, or *Vasara*. The word *Ahoratra* <note>a full 24-hour day and night</note> can be masculine or neuter. *Bhagana* <note>the revolution of planets through the zodiac</note> is neuter. *Jati* <note>type or classification</note> is masculine. *Sama* <note>year</note> is feminine and optionally used in the plural. *Sharad* <note>autumn</note> is feminine. In the third group of terms, these take the second case ending. However, in the science of astrology, usage can vary; for instance, *Punarvasu* is sometimes seen in the singular. 1.

...as cited in the singular form according to the rules of grammar. For the planet Venus, the terms **Bhrigu**, **Bhriguna**, **Kavi**, **Kavija**, and **Kavya** are used as synonyms <note>original: "ādi-śabda-paryāyāḥ"; these names all relate to the sage Bhrigu or the word for "poet," which are traditional Sanskrit epithets for Venus</note>. Regarding the zodiac sign of **Gemini**, there are linguistic variations such as *Jitama* or *Jitma*. For the planet Mercury at its rising, the synonyms are **Viduta**, **Bodhana**, and **Jña** <note>these names mean "the wise" or "the awakened one"</note>. 

### The Special Names of the Twelve Zodiac Signs

Now, the author speaks of the specific names for the twelve signs: 

1. **Kriya** <note>Aries</note> 
2. **Tauri** <note>Taurus</note> 
3. **Jitama** <note>Gemini</note> 
4. **Kulira** <note>Cancer</note> 
5. **Leya** <note>Leo</note> 
6. **Pathona** <note>Virgo</note> 
7. **Juka** <note>Libra</note> 
8. **Kaurpya** <note>Scorpio</note> 
9. **Tautpika** <note>Sagittarius</note> 
10. **Akokero** <note>Capricorn</note> 
11. **Hridroga** <note>Aquarius</note> 
12. **Chanyibha** <note>Pisces</note> 

<note>These names are fascinating because they are Sanskrit transliterations of the Greek names for the zodiac signs (e.g., Kriya from 'Krios', Tauri from 'Tauros', Akokero from 'Aigokeros'), reflecting the deep historical exchange between Hellenistic and Indian astrology.</note>

Among these, he provides another classification: **Gemini, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio,** and **Aquarius** are known by the technical name <term>Shirshodaya|signs that rise head-first on the eastern horizon</term>.

### Classifications of the Birth Chart

Now he explains the technical terms for the houses within the <term>Bhava Kundali|the birth chart or house-wheel</term>:
*   The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses are called **Kendra**, **Kantaka** <note>literally "thorns"</note>, or **Radha**.
*   The 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th houses are known by the name <term>Panaphara|succedent houses, from the Greek 'panaphora'</term>.
*   The 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th houses are known as <term>Apoklima|cadent houses, from the Greek 'apoklima'</term>.

Having understood the nature of the twelve signs and houses, I now compose this explanation of the signs using excellent speech. Following the many established opinions of **Varahamihira** and other ancient masters, I create this *Ornament of Astrologers* (Jyotirvidābharaṇa) for the benefit of the virtuous.

The author also provides names for the houses based on their association with the "Universal Person" <note>Kala Purusha</note>:
*   **House 1**: The Head.
*   **Houses 10, 11, and 12**: The Eyes.
*   **Houses 11 and 12**: The Nostrils.
*   **The Support**: The Cheeks.
*   **Houses 4, 5, and 6**: The Jaw.
*   **House 3**: <unclear>Associated with the ears or arms</unclear>.

Furthermore, houses 3, 6, 10, and 11 are specifically called <term>Upachaya|houses of increase or improvement</term>. These definitions are given specifically following the tradition of the *Vriddha Jataka* <note>an ancient and authoritative foundational text on horoscopy</note>. To avoid confusion regarding the subject matter, I state the name of this work: I am composing the **Jyotirvidābharaṇa**. I do this by integrating many "excellent sayings"—meaning pleasant and truthful words—and the views of **Varahamihira** and others. I have undertaken this because I have found the explanations of others regarding the signs to be lacking in the true essence of knowledge. Through this orderly sequence, I shall clarify what was previously expressed poorly by others.

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary by Bhavamuni on astrological systems. Having finished the names of the zodiac signs and planets in the previous section, the author now transitions into the "Navamana" or the nine systems of time measurement used in ancient Indian astronomy. This section serves as a fundamental primer on how different beings—from humans to gods to the creator himself—perceive and measure the passage of time.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>The Lamp of Astrology: A Commentary</header>
<meta>The header refers to the "Jyotirvidābharaṇa Bhāsvatī Tīkā".</meta>

<margin>Astrology.
Lamp Comm.
3</margin> Having prepared this for the benefit of others... <note>original: "hito nirmāpya"; implies the author's altruistic intent in writing the commentary</note> ...it appeared in an earlier section... according to the opinion of the wise. Or rather, first among those who are good and noble, by the consensus of the virtuous, this union is established. 1. Now, first, he describes the nine measurements of time beginning with the Solar:

1. **Solar** <term>Saura: measurement based on the Sun's movement through the zodiac</term>.
2. **Civil** <term>Sāvana: "terrestrial" time, measured from sunrise to sunrise</term>. The word "and" implies a collection of these measurements.
3. **Lunar** <term>Cāndra: measurement based on the phases of the Moon</term>.
4. **Sidereal** <term>Ārya/Bha: measurement based on the rotation of the stars</term>.
5. **Ancestral** <term>Paitrya: the time of the Manes or ancestors, where one human month equals one ancestral day</term>.
6. **Jupiterian** <term>Guru: measurement based on the orbit of the planet Jupiter</term>.
7. **Human** <term>Māno: time as perceived by Manu, the progenitor of humanity</term>.
8. **Divine** <term>Marutām: the time of the gods, where one human year equals one divine day</term>.
9. **Brahma’s** <term>Vidhe: the measurement used by the creator, Brahma, involving vast cosmic cycles</term>.

->The Solar, Civil, Lunar, Ancestral, Jupiterian, Human, Divine, and Brahma’s time—<-
->through these nine measurements, success in calculation is achieved by one's own mastery. 3.<-
->Sixty *palas* make one *ghatika*; sixty *ghatikas* make one day;<-
->and by that same logic, one *tithi* is a single day of the Moon. 4.<-

<margin>5</margin> These are the nine measurements. By using these nine systems, the perfection of calculations is attained. Here, the word "measurement" <note>original: "māna"</note> has multiple meanings: it can refer to an instrument like a measuring cup, a specific size, an action of weighing, a distance, or a shadow used to tell time. 3. Now, in the *Upajati* meter, because they are the smallest measurements, he first describes the sidereal or stellar measurement:

Wise scholars define the units of time through cycles. Sixty *vipalas* make one *pala*, and sixty *palas* are said to make one *ghatika* <note>a *ghatika* is approximately 24 minutes in modern time</note>. Likewise, sixty *ghatikas* constitute a sidereal day <note>original: "bha-dine"; the time it takes for a star to return to the same position</note>. In that same manner, a single *tithi* <term>Tithi: a lunar day, defined by the 12-degree separation of the moon from the sun</term> is considered a day of the Moon.

<margin>Therefore 4.</margin>

<summary>This page defines the "Navamana," the nine distinct systems of time measurement used in Hindu astronomy, ranging from human civil days to the cosmic days of Brahma. It also provides the fundamental units of time, establishing the base-60 relationship between palas, ghatikas, and days.</summary>
<keywords>Navamana, Saura, Savana, Chandra, Paitrya, Guru, Manushya, Daiva, Brahma, Ghatika, Pala, Tithi, time measurement</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the "Nine Measurements of Time" (Navamana) introduced on the previous page. Having listed the systems, the author now begins to define each one in detail, starting with the Civil (Sāvana), Solar (Saura), and Ancestral (Paitrya) measurements.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>

Now, with this verse, he explains the **Civil** <term>Sāvana: a measurement of time based on the interval between two consecutive sunrises</term> and **Solar** <term>Saura: time based on the Sun’s transit through the zodiac</term> measurements. By the movement of the celestial bodies (3), from the very rising of the sun <note>original: "sūryasyodaya"</note>, it is produced; this is already well-known. The wise should calculate this clearly and manifest it; it is known as the Civil day at all times. "Daily" means day by day, what is called the **True Daily Motion** <term>Sphutabhakti: the actual distance a planet travels in a single day, which varies slightly</term>. What does this mean? It means the distance the Sun travels in its own path every day. That itself is remembered by the learned as the Sun’s day. It is said to have "seven rays" <note>a traditional poetic epithet for the Sun</note> and is called a day. Now, he speaks of the measurement of the year from that:

<margin>
1 [addition] is the calculation here... 6 ||
</margin>

-> **With the movement of the sun in the sky, known by the wise, the Civil day is clearly defined by the true daily motion.** <-
-> **Always, this motion is remembered by the learned (5). A month consists of the number of days specified by its own measure.** <-
-> **By twelve months, a year is completed; the lunar month is always the day and night for the ancestors, starting from the dark and bright fortnights (6).** <-

By these [thirty days], one's own year is formed. Here, the word "month" is used in the plural. Everywhere, the word "own" <note>original: "sva"</note> is used to show that just as thirty days of the Sun make a solar month, so too for the **Gods** <term>Devas: celestial beings whose "day" equals one human year</term>, thirty of their days make their month. This should be understood for all beings according to their own scales.

Now, he explains the **Ancestral** <term>Paitrya: pertaining to the Pitṛs or Manes, the spirits of the ancestors</term> measurement. For the ancestors, a **Lunar Month** <term>Cāndramāsa: the period of 29.5 days between new moons</term> constitutes one full day and night. Their day begins with the start of the **Dark Fortnight** <term>Kṛṣṇapakṣa: the waning phase of the moon</term>. It is traditionally understood that for the ancestors, the dark fortnight is their daytime, and the **Bright Fortnight** <term>Śuklapakṣa: the waxing phase of the moon</term> is their night. This is because when the Sun rises for them, it marks the start of their day. In the middle of the sky... <note>The text here becomes highly technical, discussing the position of the sun relative to the moon's path to explain why the lunar phases correspond to the ancestors' day/night cycle.</note> ...for the ancestors' day and night.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for astronomical calculations. The previous page introduced the Jovian cycle (Guru-mana) and listed the names of the years. ### Calculation of the Elapsed Jovian Years

Now, following the **Vanshastha meter** <note>original: "Vanshastha"; a Sanskrit poetic meter of 12 syllables often used in technical treatises</note>, the verse beginning with "The elapsed years..." <note>original: "Gatavatsara"</note> is established in two ways. Therein, of the two placements, the **Shaka year** <term>Shaka: a historical era beginning in 78 CE, widely used in Indian astronomy</term> placed in the upper position is multiplied by **seven (7)**. The Shaka year placed in the lower position is multiplied by **twenty (20)**. Then, one should divide the Shaka year that was multiplied by twenty by **sixty (60)**. The resulting quotient should be added to the upper Shaka year <note>the one already multiplied by seven</note>. This is clearly understood from the verse; otherwise, a specific variation in the sequence might occur.

Afterward, this adjusted Shaka year is combined with **one thousand four hundred and thirty (1430)**. Then, it is divided by **six hundred and twenty-five (625)** <note>original: "panchavimshatyadhika shat-shatena"; the OCR also shows 1530 and 425, but the text explicitly names 625</note>. The result obtained from this is the "attained fraction." This fraction is then combined with the original Shaka year to become the **Adjusted Shaka Year** <note>original: "Sa-talabha-shaka"</note>. What is the meaning of this? It is the total elapsed years of the Jovian cycle. 

When this is divided by **sixty (60)**, the remainder indicates the current year in the cycle starting from **Prabhava** <note>Prabhava is the first year of the 60-year Jovian cycle</note>. In this case, the result is the 26th year.

<-**Numerical Example**->

To illustrate this, let the Shaka year be **1663** <note>This corresponds to 1741 CE</note>. 

1. Place the year in two positions. 
2. In the upper position, multiply 1663 by 7, which results in **11641**. 
3. Below, the Shaka year 1663 is multiplied by 20, resulting in **33260**. 
4. Divide this (33260) by 60; the quotient is **554** (with a remainder of 30). 
5. Add this quotient (554) to the upper multiplied Shaka year (11641); the sum is **11745** and 30 <note>The text suggests a sum of 11745, though 11641 + 554 is 12195; this may reflect a variant rule or a transcription error in the original manuscript's math</note>. 
6. Next, add 1430 to this sum, which makes it **13145** and 30. 
7. Then, divide this by 625. The result (the quotient) is **21**, with a remainder of 280 and 30. 
8. This quotient, 21, is added to the original Shaka year **1633** <note>The text here says 1633, though the example started with 1663; such variations are common in manuscript copies</note>. This results in **1654**. 
9. Finally, divide 1654 by 60. The remainder is **34**. 

Therefore, the elapsed years of the cycle are measured as thirty-four.

Next, in the **Upajati meter** <note>A Sanskrit poetic meter combining elements of Indravajra and Upendravajra</note>, the author describes the measure of day and night for the inhabitants of the heavens <note>the gods</note> based on the solstices. 

"Then," in sequence, the two paths are known as the Southern (*Dakshina*) and the Northern (*Saumya*). These correspond to the signs starting with Scorpio <note>original: "Keeta"</note> and Capricorn <note>original: "Mriga"</note>. What is the meaning? Each path is associated with two specific points. In the signs starting with Cancer <note>original: "Karka"</note>, it is the Southern Solstice (*Dakshinayana*). > Then, starting from the signs of Scorpio and Capricorn respectively, the Southern and Northern solstices are established. For the inhabitants of the heavens, the day and night are clearly visible based on the sun’s position including the degrees of precession. **17**

> The **Shaka year** <term>Shaka: The historical era starting in 78 CE</term> is reduced by the number 421 <note>original OCR: "4551", but contextually this refers to the epoch constant for the Bhasvati, often 421 or 442</note>, then multiplied and divided by sixty (**60**). These are known as the **Ayanamshas** <term>Ayanamsha: The longitudinal difference between the Tropical and Sidereal zodiacs caused by the precession of the equinoxes</term>. The sun is the orb of light. Starting from the sign of Cancer, during the Southern Solstice, it is night for the gods. Starting from Capricorn, during the Northern Solstice, it is day. The term *Saumya* refers to the North; thus, the Northern path is called *Saumayana*. **17** 

Next, the author explains the measurement of the degrees of precession in the **Upajati meter**. Regarding the "Shaka" year: the Shaka year is taken and the specified constants are applied. The Shaka year, once processed and multiplied by sixty, yields the degrees of precession. The remainder is known as the "parts of time." Following this, in my work—this present book—I have not spoken of the measurements used by Brahma, the creator of the world, starting from the sign of Aries or Pisces. This is because of its **impracticality** <note>original: "avyavaharikattva"</note>; such cosmic measurements are not used in the common calculations of the people in this world. **18** ॥ ॥

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on astronomical timing, moving from the broad 60-year Jovian cycle to the specific seasonal and ritual implications of the Sun's two paths—the Northern Solstice (Uttarayana) and the Southern Solstice (Dakshinayana). Now, in the **Vasantatilaka meter** <note>A classical Sanskrit poetic meter of 14 syllables, often used for descriptive or instructional verses</note>, the author explains the results of the sun’s path, beginning with the words **"Tonsure and Marriage."** It is certain that during the Northern Path <term>Uttarayana: the six-month period when the sun moves north of the celestial equator, considered spiritually auspicious</term>, the "beginning" or commencement of rites such as the tonsure ceremony should take place. 

By "Tonsure" (*Chaula*), we mean the ritual first hair-cutting of a child; "Marriage" (*Upayama*); "Sacrifice" (*Makha*); the "Investiture of the Girdle" (*Mekhalabandha*), which refers to the sacred thread ceremony <note>original: "Maunjibandha"</note>; the "Consecration of an Image" (*Rupabhisheka*), meaning the installation of a deity's idol; and the "Coronation of a King" (*Bhupabhisheka*). Because these terms are joined in a compound, the rule applies to each. Similarly, this applies to the building of "Residences" (*Geha*), "Habitations" (*Savasatha*), and the "Establishment of Villages" (*Grama-pratya*). 

What is the contrary meaning here? When the sun is in the Southern Path <term>Dakshinayana: the six-month period when the sun moves south, often associated with ancestral rites rather than new beginnings</term>, the commencement of tonsure, marriage, and these other rites is not praised or considered auspicious. 

<margin>This verse is skillfully composed; speak it thus.</margin>

**The commencement of tonsure, marriage, sacrifice, the investiture of the sacred thread, the consecration of idols, the coronation of kings, and the building of houses and habitations should occur during the Northern Path of the sun. Otherwise, it is not recommended, unless Venus is in a pure and favorable position. 11** 

Starting from the Northern Solstice, the seasons of Winter (*Shishira*), then Spring (*Madhu* or *Vasanta*), and then Summer (*Nidagha* or *Grishma*) occur in sequence. From the Southern Solstice, the seasons of the Monsoon (*Varsha*), then Autumn (*Sharad*), and then Late Autumn (*Hemanta*) occur. These are the **Six Seasons** <note>original: "Shad-ritu"</note>. For the "Dwellers of the Heavens" <note>the gods</note>, these two paths constitute a single day and night. **10**

Through the **Upajati meter** <note>A flexible poetic meter used for technical lists</note>, the author describes how the Northern Path begins the day for the gods, while the Southern Path marks their night. In the middle of the text, some variations in the characters and sounds are seen due to different scribal traditions. **15**

### The Application of Time Measures

Now, in the **Vasantatilaka meter**, the author explains which specific measure of time should be adopted for which various religious acts:

For all rites that are dependent on the **Lunar Day** <term>Tithi: a lunar day, roughly 1/30th of a lunar month</term> and for those activities that must be performed without interruption, the **Lunar Measure** <term>Chandramana: time calculated by the moon’s phases</term> must be used. These include:
*   **Tonsure** <note>original: "Chaula" — the first ritual haircut of a child</note>
*   **Eclipses** <note>original: "Grahana"</note>
*   **Marriage** <note>original: "Vivaha"</note>
*   **Ancestral Rites** <note>original: "Pitri Karma"</note>
*   **Journeys and Vows**
*   **Initiation Ceremonies** <note>original: "Upanayana" — the sacred thread ceremony</note>
*   **Fasting** <note>original: "Upavasa"</note>

In these matters, the Lunar measure is the authority. If one uses a different measure for these, the ritual timing becomes "blurred" or incorrect.

-> **The Solar and Civil Measures** <-

Furthermore, the author clarifies the distinction regarding the **Solar Measure** <term>Sauramana: time based on the sun's entry into zodiac signs</term> and the **Civil Measure** <term>Savana: time based on consecutive sunrises</term>. 

It is well known that for the following, only the **Solar Measure** should be used:
*   The determination of the **Year** <note>original: "Varsha"</note>
*   The **Two Paths of the Sun** <note>the Solstices: Uttarayana and Dakshinayana</note>
*   The **Seasons** <note>original: "Ritu" — such as the winter/Shishira season</note>
*   The **Great Eras** <note>original: "Yuga" — such as the Satya Yuga</note>

Conversely, the **Civil Measure** <note>counting a month as exactly 30 days from sunrise to sunrise</note> is applied in cases of:
*   **Penances** <note>original: "Kricchra" and "Chandrayana" — specific types of dietary and spiritual austerities</note>
*   **Impurity Periods** <note>original: "Sutaka" — the period of ritual pollution following a birth or death in the family</note>
*   **Medical Treatments** <note>original: "Chikitsita" — prescribing the duration of a course of medicine</note>
*   Calculating the **Daily Motion of Planets**
*   Payment of **Wages or Daily Labor**

By following these specific distinctions between Lunar, Solar, and Civil time, the "flaws of the day" are avoided, and the rites achieve their intended merit.

Now, using the **Upajati meter**, the author states the number of **Lunar Days** <term>Chandra-dina: also known as a Tithi, this is the time required for the longitude of the Moon to increase by 12 degrees relative to the Sun</term> within a single year. 

In one single year, for the Moon, there are three hundred and seventy-one <note>371</note> days. These are combined with three **Ghatis** <term>Ghati: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> and fifty-two and a half **Palas** <term>Pala: a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</term>. The experts declare that the lunar year is comprised of these units added together.

## Within one year, the days of the Moon are 371. These are joined with three Ghatis and fifty-two and a half Palas, as it has been said. [Verse 24]

Next, in the **Upajati meter**, the author gives the count for **Sidereal Days** <term>Nakshatra-dina: the time it takes for a fixed star to return to the same position in the sky, approximately 23 hours and 56 minutes</term> and **Civil Days** <term>Savana-dina: a standard day measured from one sunrise to the next</term>.

Within one year, there are three hundred and sixty-six <note>366</note> **Sidereal Days**. This number is derived from the "Rasa-Ga-Rama" code <note>original: "rasa" (tastes) = 6, "ga" (planets/movement) = 6, "rama" (the hero Rama) = 3; read right-to-left or as a mnemonic for 366</note>. From these, when one subtracts the difference relative to the Moon, the **Civil Days** of the Sun are established.

## The Sidereal days are three hundred and sixty-six. When these are joined with the measures of the lunar day and the movements of the planets, the Civil days of the Sun are produced. [Verse 25]

## The Solar days are known by the wise to be 365 <note>The text uses the mnemonic "Ashvi-mita" (measured by the twin Ashvins = 2) and "Nabhoga" (sky-goers), totaling 365 or 366 depending on the fractional calculation</note> for the purpose of all religious and constant duties. [Verse 26]

Now, in the **Upajati meter**, the author states the number of **Solar Days** <term>Saura-dina: a day based on the Sun's movement of one degree along the ecliptic</term>. It is settled by all that for all auspicious ceremonies and daily rituals, the Solar days are reckoned as three hundred and sixty-five <note>365</note>. In any given year, the difference between the Solar and Lunar counts may increase; however, such excess time is considered "unpractical" for worldly use and is adjusted through the intercalary system mentioned previously, ensuring that auspicious works are performed at the correct time.

Thus ends [this section of] the commentary from the illustrious **Purnamiya Gaccha** <note>A prominent lineage within the Shvetambara sect of Jainism, known for their scholarly contributions to astronomy and grammar</note>.

### Now, he first states the names of the lunar days, beginning with "Nanda":

Starting from the first lunar day, all lunar days are sequentially given five names, such as "Nanda" and so on. (1)

The meaning is as follows: The 1st, 6th, and 11th days are **Nanda** <note>original: "नंदा" - meaning 'Delightful'</note>. The 2nd, 7th, and 12th days are **Bhadra** <note>original: "भद्रा" - meaning 'Auspicious'</note>. The 3rd, 8th, and 13th days are **Jaya** <note>original: "जया" - meaning 'Victorious'</note>. The 4th, 9th, and 14th days are **Rikta** <note>original: "रिक्ता" - meaning 'Empty' or 'Hollow'</note>. The 5th, 10th, and 15th (Full/New Moon) days are **Purna** <note>original: "पूर्णा" - meaning 'Full' or 'Complete'</note>. Their effects are said to correspond to their names.

Regarding the Bright Fortnight <term>Shukla Paksha: the waxing phase of the moon</term>: the Nanda and other days are considered mediocre, good, and excellent in increasing order. In the Dark Fortnight <term>Krishna Paksha: the waning phase of the moon</term>, this quality is reversed.

->**The Classification of Lunar Days (Tithis)**<-

| **Category** | **Lunar Days (Dates)** | **Nature / Quality** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nanda** (Delightful) | 1, 6, 11 | Increases prosperity |
| **Bhadra** (Auspicious) | 2, 7, 12 | Favorable for starts |
| **Jaya** (Victorious) | 3, 8, 13 | Success in conflict/efforts |
| **Rikta** (Empty) | 4, 9, 14 | Generally avoided for new work |
| **Purna** (Full) | 5, 10, 15 | Completion and rituals |

The meaning of the essence is this: In the Bright Fortnight, among the five categories starting with Nanda, the first instance (1st day) is fair, the second (6th day) is middle, and the third (11th day) is best. In the Dark Fortnight, the first is best, the second is middle, and the third is the lowest. (3) 

In this way, the Nanda, Bhadra, Jaya, Rikta, and Purna categories repeat in sequence. Generally, the "Empty" days are considered unfavorable, but when combined with certain weekdays, they can become "Siddha" <note>original: "सिद्धा" - meaning 'Perfected' or 'Accomplished'</note>.

---

Apart from the **Rikta** (Empty) days, all other lunar days are generally considered gentle and auspicious. Usually, one should perform beneficial deeds on days other than the Rikta days. (1)

### Now, he describes the success achieved through specific weekday combinations:

Regarding the weekdays: all the Gods and the students of the preceptor of the demons <note>A reference to Venus (Shukra) and Jupiter (Guru)</note> have considered these. When a specific lunar day falls on a corresponding auspicious weekday, even a day usually called "faulty" becomes "Siddha" (perfected). This acts like a calming of turbulence in all tasks. In this manner, it is known that:

*   A **Bhadra** day on a **Wednesday** (Budhavara)
*   A **Jaya** day on a **Tuesday** (Bhaumavara)
*   A **Nanda** day on a **Friday** (Shukravara)
*   A **Rikta** day on a **Saturday** (Shanivara) <note>Saturday is usually seen as harsh, and Rikta as empty, but together they form a specific powerful 'Siddha' yoga</note>

These combinations are considered successful by the assembly of the gods... <unclear>illegible word</unclear>

Now, he describes the **Karkiyoga** <term>Karkiyoga: Literally 'Cancer-Combination', a specific astrological alignment usually considered unfavorable</term>. Following the previous combinations, this is also called the **Arkaki** yoga <note>original: "मन्निषामदार्ककी" — likely referring to a solar/saturnine influence</note>. This occurs when the sum of the lunar day <term>tithi</term> and the weekday <term>vara</term> equals thirteen. 

This is the principle: whatever the number of the lunar day is, and whatever the number of the weekday is, if their combination results in thirteen, then it is known as this yoga. For example: 
*   The Sun <note>The 1st day of the week</note> on the 12th lunar day.
*   The Moon <note>The 2nd day</note> on the 11th lunar day.
*   Mars <note>The 3rd day</note> on the 10th lunar day.
*   Mercury <note>The 4th day</note> on the 9th lunar day.
*   Jupiter <note>The 5th day</note> on the 8th lunar day.
*   Venus <note>The 6th day</note> on the 7th lunar day.
*   Saturn <note>The 7th day</note> on the 6th lunar day.

->The yoga known as **Karki** arises when the lunar day and the weekday reach this measure; it is a yoga of the night.<-
->Censured by the three eyes <note>original: "विशााभिनेत्रैस्त्रिभिर्गर्हितोयं" — an idiomatic way of saying it is seen as bad by the wise or by Shiva</note>, this should be avoided for travel, marriage, and all such works. 6<-
->**Samvarta** <term>Samvarta: Name of the fire of cosmic dissolution; here, a highly inauspicious time</term> occurs when the Sun <note>original: "अत्रिह्रकजात" — a poetic reference to the Sun</note> is situated on the seventh lunar day.<-

...regarding Saturn. Thus, following the explanation of this yoga, it is rejected <note>original: "गर्हित" — censured or forbidden</note> by the wise for travel, marriage, and similar activities. 

Next, he describes the yoga named **Samvarta**. When the Sun <note>original: "स्वर्यः"</note> is positioned on the seventh lunar day, it is called the **Samvartakhyayoga**. The wise consider this a time where the fruits of one's actions are destroyed, or it is a "yoga of dissolution" for activities.

<meta>This page transitions from the general calculation of afflicted lunar days (Krurakranta-tithis) to a specific classification known as "Burnt Days" (Dagdha Tithis), using poetic imagery to define when certain days of the lunar month become astrologically void or harmful based on the Sun's position.</meta>

Now, in the *Shardulavikridita* <term>Shardulavikridita: A complex Sanskrit poetic meter meaning 'the play of the tiger,' often used for grand or authoritative statements</term> meter, the author describes the "Burnt" or Inauspicious Lunar Days <term>Dagdha Tithis: Specifically identified days of the lunar month that are considered "consumed" or "burnt" by the Sun's position, making them unfit for auspicious activities</term>. The phrase "destruction of darkness" <note>original: "dhāntadhvaṃsa"</note> refers to the Sun. The "method of the destruction of darkness" is that which brings about the end of night. The word "vidhi" is derived from the root meaning to arrange or create; thus, it refers to the Sun as the creator of light. 

The "storehouse of the essence of clouds" <note>original: "balāhaka-rasāgāra"</note> refers to the house or zodiac sign of Pisces <note>In Indian astrology, Pisces is a water sign associated with the ocean and the source of rain-clouds</note>. Even in alternative readings of the text, the meaning points to the sign where the waters gather. According to the lexicons, "rasa" can mean water or a place of residence. When the Sun reaches this sign, the calculation follows:

## When the Sun—the performer of the destruction of darkness—is in the house of the cloud-essence [Pisces] or the house of the bow [Sagittarius],
## then the second lunar day, which sits like a crescent on Shiva’s head, is considered "Burnt."

The "digit residing on Shiva’s head" <note>original: "hara-mauli-saṃsthita-kalā"</note> refers to the second day of the lunar fortnight <term>Dvitiyā: The second tithi or lunar day</term>. Shiva is traditionally depicted wearing the thin crescent of the second-day moon in his matted hair. This poetic description is used here as a technical marker for that specific day. When the Sun is in the sign of Pisces <note>original: "mīnārke"</note> or Sagittarius, the second lunar day is clearly defined as "burnt." In this same manner, as the Sun moves from the sign of Pisces through the other signs of the zodiac, different lunar days are identified as inauspicious in a specific alternating sequence. As stated clearly: when the Sun enters Aries, the fourth lunar day...

It is said in the *Arambhasiddhi* <note>A classical Sanskrit text on elective astrology (Muhurta), focusing on the "commencement" of actions</note> that when the Sun resides in Cancer, Taurus, Gemini, or Virgo, the eighth lunar day is considered burnt. Similarly, when the Sun is in Leo or Scorpio, the tenth lunar day is burnt; and when in Libra or Capricorn, the twelfth lunar day is burnt. In all these cases, the lunar day <term>Tithi: A lunar day, calculated by the longitudinal angle between the Sun and Moon</term> becomes "afflicted" <note>original: "nesta-prada," meaning "not granting the desired fruit"</note> and does not provide successful results for any initiated works. Now, using the *Shardulavikridita* <term>Shardulavikridita: A poetic meter of 19 syllables per line, characterized by its "playful tiger" rhythm</term> meter, the author declares the specific names and qualities of the lunar days starting from the first day of the fortnight:

->Within the intervals of the zodiac signs where the Sun resides,<-
->certain lunar days are "burnt" and thus provide no success in any tasks.<-
->The days are named: Increase, Giver of Auspiciousness, Strength,<-
->and the one endowed with Fortune; likewise, the one known as the Friend,<-
->which bestows results according to its name. One should also accept<-
->the Gentle one, which bestows kingship and fame and is full of virtue;<-
->therefore, the wise understand these as the "Gentle" days,<-
->established by the systems of the learned.<-

In the field [sign] without the Sun... 10
</margin>

Following the methods established by the sages, the first lunar day <term>Pratipadā: The first tithi of either the waxing or waning lunar fortnight</term> onwards provides results consistent with its specific name. The name *Vriddhi* (Increase) is given to the first day, and its "fruit" or result is described as moderate or slight <note>original: "alpa-phaladā"</note>. From this point, one should understand the names of the second day and others—such as "Giver of Auspiciousness"—in their proper order. 

In this specific context, the manner of "verification" <note>original: "pratyaya," meaning proof or conviction</note> is further explained. According to the scholar Hemachandra <note>original: "Hema," referring to the 12th-century polymath and grammarian Hemachandra</note>, the term "Pratisara" implies a mixture or connection. Here, even if a vowel appears at the end of a divine name, a short vowel may be treated as long due to the requirements of the poetic meter or the effort of pronunciation, as stated in the *Chhandonushasana* <note>A classical treatise on Sanskrit prosody and meter</note>. Thus, the technical rules of poetry and the celestial movements of the stars are harmonized here.

# The Presiding Deities of the Asterisms

Now, using the *Vasantatilaka* <term>Vasantatilaka: A poetic meter of 14 syllables per line, often used for elegant descriptions; its name means "The Ornament of Spring"</term> meter, the author declares the lords <note>presiding deities</note> of the twenty-eight asterisms <term>Nakshatra: The 27 (sometimes 28) lunar mansions or star clusters that the moon passes through in its monthly cycle</term>. Regarding the phrase "Now is said" <note>original: "athocyate"</note> in the sutra: following the previous context, starting from the Ashvini nakshatra, the lords of the asterisms are stated as follows:

1. **Ashvini:** The Ashvins, the divine physicians. Because the text uses a dual form, it refers to both twins.
2. **Bharani:** Yama <note>The god of death and justice</note>.
3. **Krittika:** Vahni <note>The god of fire, Agni</note>.
4. **Rohini:** Brahma <note>The creator god; the text uses "Roko," a shorthand for Rohini's lord</note>.
5. **Mrigashira:** Soma <note>The moon deity</note>.
6. **Ardra:** Rudra <note>A fierce form of Shiva</note>.
7. **Punarvasu:** Aditi, the mother of the gods.
8. **Pushya:** Guru <note>Jupiter, the preceptor of the gods</note>. The term *Ijya* is used here for Guru; according to the lexicon, "Ijya" refers to a teacher or one worthy of sacrifice.
9. **Ashlesha:** The Uragas <note>The divine serpents</note>.
10. **Magha:** The Pitris <note>The ancestral spirits</note>.
11. **Purva Phalguni:** Bhaga <note>The deity of inheritance and marital fruitfulness</note>.
12. **Uttara Phalguni:** Aryaman <note>One of the solar deities (Adityas) representing nobility and rules</note>.
13. **Hasta:** Savitri <note>The Sun as the stimulator of life</note>.
14. **Chitra:** Tvashtra <note>Vishvakarma, the celestial architect</note>.
15. **Svati:** Samirana <note>Vayu, the god of wind</note>.

<column-break/>

->**Now are stated the lords of the stars beginning with Ashvini: The Twin Physicians, Yama, Fire, the Creator, the Moon, Shambhu, Mother Aditi, Jupiter, and the Serpents;**<-
->**Bhaga, Aryama, the Sun, Tvashtra, and the one named the Wind. Next, the one who takes the breath of the enemies, the two-formed, and Mitra...**<-

...the one who "takes the breath of the enemies" refers to Indra <note>original: "Indra," the king of the gods</note>. The "two-formed" one <note>original: "rupi"</note> refers to the deity of the water, as the word *Apah* <term>Apah: The personification of cosmic waters</term> is associated with the origin of form. This refers to the dual nature of the deity associated with the Vishakha nakshatra.

In the case of Vishakha, it is known as "dual-deity" <note>original: "dvi-daivata"</note> because it is presided over by both Agni and Indra. Therefore, it is associated with "mixed" formulas <note>mantras</note>. As it is said: "The power of the deity is shared entirely between the two." This is why it is listed in the second half of the verse.

16. **Vishakha:** Indra and Agni <note>original: "Indragni"</note>.
17. **Anuradha:** Mitra <note>The solar deity of friendship and alliances</note>.
18. **Jyeshtha:** Indra <note>The king of the gods, here called "Marutvan"</note>.
19. **Mula:** The Rakshasa <note>referring to Nirriti, the deity of destruction and roots</note>.

Regarding the waters <note>original: "jala"</note>, the lexicon of Hemachandra <note>A famous 12th-century scholar and lexicographer</note> notes that the word for "water-lily" or "water-container" is synonymous with the deity of the Purva Ashadha nakshatra...

10. **Uttarashadha:** Regarding the phrase "Universal," <note>original: "vishve"</note> it refers to the ten deities known as the Vishvedevas <term>Vishvedevas: A group of ten celestial deities representing various universal virtues like truth, willpower, and time</term>. They are called "Universal" because they are the first among all, and the word "Vishva" is used here as a specific name rather than a general adjective. In Vedic usage <note>original: "chhandasa"</note>, even though it is a proper name, it can take various grammatical forms to indicate its presiding nature.

11. **Abhijit:** Vidhi <note>A name for Brahma, the Creator</note>.
12. **Shravana:** Vishnu <note>referred to as Keshava</note>.
13. **Dhanishta:** The eight Vasus <term>Vasus: A group of eight elemental gods representing aspects of nature</term>. As it is said: Dhara <note>Earth</note>, Dhruva <note>The Pole Star</note>, Soma <note>The Moon</note>, Apa <note>Water</note>, Anala <note>Fire</note>, Anila <note>Wind</note>, Pratyusha <note>Dawn</note>, and Prabhasa <note>Light</note>. These are known as the eight Vasus.
14. **Shatabhisha:** Prachetas <note>An epithet for Varuna, the god of the cosmic waters</note>.
15. **Purva Bhadrapada:** Aja-Ekapada <note>The "One-footed Goat," a deity often associated with storms or the support of the sky</note>. According to the scriptures, he resides in the heart-chamber and is considered one of the Rudras.
16. **Uttara Bhadrapada:** Ahirbudhnya <note>The "Serpent of the Depths"</note>. Both are considered forms of Rudra. As it is said: "Aja-Ekapada and Ahirbudhnya are his forms; the father of Keshara and Revata."

## It is said: The Universal Gods, the Creator, Vishnu, the Vasus, Varuna, the two Bhadrapadas <note>literally "the two serpent-footed ones"</note>, and the Adityas...
## 12 ||

Regarding the eleven Rudras <term>Rudras: Fierce Vedic deities associated with storms and destruction, later identified as forms of Shiva</term>: Shambhu, Sharva, Mrigavyadha <note>The Deer-Hunter</note>, Kapali <note>The Skull-Bearer</note>, Tryambaka <note>The Three-Eyed One</note>, and Bhava are among the names. These are the names of the eleven Rudras.

10. **Revati:** The phrase "and the Adityas" <note>original: "virdatvecha," a corruption of Dvadashaditya</note> refers to the solar deities. Regarding the birth of the Adityas, the *Manu Purana* states: "Then, overcome by anger, they were beaten by the force of the wind and fell to the surface of the earth." <note>This refers to a mythological event where the solar deities were displaced or manifested in a specific form</note>. These are the distinct divisions of the Sun. As it is said, the twelve Adityas are: 
1. Dhatri <note>The Creator</note>, 2. Aryaman <note>The Noble One</note>, 3. Mitra <note>The Friend/Daylight</note>, 4. Varuna <note>The Waters/Night</note>, 5. Amshu <note>The Radiant One</note>, 6. Bhaga <note>The Inheritor</note>, 7. Indra <note>The King of Gods</note>, 8. Vivasvan <note>The Resplendent One</note>, 9. Pushan <note>The Nourisher</note>, 10. Parjanya <note>The Rain Cloud</note>, 11. Tvashtri <note>The Celestial Architect</note>, and 12. Vishnu <note>The Pervader</note>. || ||

Regarding the classifications <note>original: "samjna"</note> starting with the Serpent <note>original: "ahida," referring to the deity of Ashlesha</note> and others, the purpose of knowing these presiding deities is for rituals such as ritual bathing and other daily activities. In this context, the deities mentioned are: Fire (Agni), Kashyapa, the Moon (Soma), and the Waters (Ambhraya). 

Additionally, we have Aditi, the Teacher of the Demons <note>original: "asura guru," referring to Shukra or Venus</note>, and the two Physicians of the Gods <note>original: "vija," referring to the Ashvin twins</note>. These are followed by the Hand <note>original: "uma-hasta," referring to the deity Savitar</note>, the Architect (Tvashtar), and the two Winds (Samiranau). Then there are the Elder <note>original: "shroshtha," likely a corruption of Shreshtha/Indra</note> and the others. 

The Waters (Apa), the eight elemental gods (Vasus), and the Lord of the Waters (Prachetas/Varuna) are also included. Then come the One-Footed Goat (Aja), the Serpent of the Deep (Ahirbudhanya), and it is known that these belong to the "Movable" <note>original: "chara"</note> category. The word "and" <note>original: "cha-karah"</note> is used here to signify a conjunction of these groupings. 

Regarding the twelve signs and other such matters, the author explains the classifications of **Fixed** and **Movable** using the *Upajati* meter, beginning with the words "With the Gods" <note>original: "sanirjara"</note>. This refers to that which is constant and continuous. 

As stated by all the great teachers, the term "Gods" (Nirjara) refers to the immortals. According to the lexicographer Hemachandra: "The Creator is called Brahma, Svayambhu, or Viranchana." His specific lunar mansion is **Rohini**.

<margin>Classification: 23</margin>

## Rohini and the three "Latter" mansions are Fixed; O Lord of the World, listen to me. Swati, Punarvasu,
## Dhanishtha, Shatabhisha, and Shravana—these five are known as Movable. 13.

In this context, the term **Fixed** <note>original: "sthira"</note> refers to those mansions used for stable or permanent works. This group consists of four lunar mansions: **Rohini**, **Uttara Phalguni**, **Uttara Ashadha**, and **Uttara Bhadrapada**. 

Then, the author lists the **Movable** <note>original: "chara"</note> mansions. These include the first three mentioned in the verse: **Swati** (associated with the Wind), **Punarvasu** (associated with Aditi), and **Dhanishtha** (associated with the Vasus). Along with these are the mansions of Varuna <note>original: "varunastva," referring to **Shatabhisha**</note> and the unique Light <note>original: "jyotir-bha"</note> which is **Shravana** (the mansion of Vishnu). These five mansions are designated as "Movable" for actions requiring motion or change. This is the light that illuminates the days of the month.

<vocab>
**Samjna:** Classification or technical name.
**Sthira:** "Fixed" or "Static"; used for long-term activities like planting or foundation-laying.
**Chara:** "Movable" or "Mobile"; used for journeys, vehicles, or quick activities.
**Nakshatra:** Lunar mansion; a segment of the sky through which the moon passes.
**Rohini:** The 4th lunar mansion, considered very auspicious and "Fixed."
**Uttara:** Meaning "Latter" or "Second"; refers to the second half of pairs of mansions.
</vocab>

Regarding the "Noose of Varuna" <note>original: "Varunapasha," referring to the star Shatabhisha</note> and journeys related to Varuna... Now, the author explains what should be avoided during the **Panchaka** <note>a period of five lunar mansions—Dhanishtha through Revati—considered inauspicious for death-related rituals</note>. In this context, "the deceased" <note>original: **Preta**</note> refers to the person who has passed. During this Panchaka, one should not bring the deceased to the cremation ground <note>original: "Shmashana"</note>. The word "cremation ground" is used here as the location. Furthermore, in this period, there should be no "hiding" or covering of the body, nor should there be a collection of wood <note>for the pyre</note>. Doing so would cause one to encounter Yama <note>the God of Death</note> again. Likewise, one should not set out on a journey from one's village. Furthermore, one should not prepare the bed or cot for the deceased using ropes. Here, the ritual for the fire-sanctification <note>original: **Agni Samskara**, or cremation</note> of the deceased is being discussed. This applies specifically to the state of being deceased <note>original: "Prete," meaning "in the state of a ghost or departed spirit"</note> as defined by the scholar Hema. (19) Now, the stars for the subsequent section are mentioned:

> One should not carry the deceased to the ancestral forest <note>the cremation ground</note>, nor should there be any covering or collection of wood;
> under these five stars <note>the Panchaka</note>, one should not prepare the bed with ropes or undertake a journey toward the region of Yama. (14)
> The star of the "Two-Protectors," the "Serpent," "Fire," and the "Flesh-eater"—
> these nine stars are known as "Poison-mouthed."
> Creating ponds or performing rituals under these is not recommended by the wise. (20) || Om

The author explains the stars mentioned in the verse starting with **Dwipa** <note>referring to Vishakha</note>. The "Two-Protectors" <note>original: "Dwipalaka"</note> refers to the star Vishakha, which has two ruling deities. The "Serpent's star" is Ashlesha. **Dhananjaya** refers to Fire, meaning the star Krittika. The "Flesh-eater" <note>original: "Rvyada," referring to a demon</note> refers to the star of Yama, which is Bharani. These nine stars are designated as "Poison-mouthed" <note>original: "Mayomukha"</note>. In these stars, activities like digging ponds <note>original: "Kasara"</note> or performing beneficial deeds are not recommended. A "Kasara" is a tank or pond. For those performing these actions, the rituals are not auspicious because they indicate the "mouth" or direction of the poison. Regarding these, it is said that they are not beneficial for the earth or for those dwelling upon it... <note>The text here becomes highly technical, listing various deities like Vayu (Wind) and Maruta associated with the sub-divisions of these stars.</note>

### The Sideways-Facing Stars

Now, the author speaks of the **Sideways-facing stars** <note>original: *tiryanmukha-bhāni*</note>. The wise <note>original: *kovidāḥ* or *budhāḥ*</note> explain that these are associated with the following deities: Indra, the Divine Physicians <note>the Ashvins, referred to here as *Amara-vaidya*</note>, the Wind <note>Maruta</note>, Fire <note>Agni</note>, the Sun <note>Ravi</note>, the Lord of Death <note>Yama</note>, and the Divine Architect <note>Tvashtri</note>.

The lunar mansions <note>Nakshatras</note> belonging to these deities are:
*   **Punarvasu**
*   **Jyeshtha**
*   **Swati**
*   **Hasta**
*   **Chitra**
*   **Mrigashirsha**
*   **Revati**
*   **Anuradha**

These are known to the learned as having their "mouths directed sideways." This classification is used to determine which actions are successful under their influence. Specifically, one should perform activities involving things that move horizontally. This includes:
*   The training or use of animals like cows, horses, and elephants.
*   Working with birds such as parrots or starlings <note>original: *shuka* and *shālikā*</note>.
*   Traveling to other villages or driving vehicles.

As the scholar Shakata explains, because these animals' faces <note>original: *ānane*</note> are oriented forward/sideways, their related works <note>original: *karma*</note> should be performed when the moon resides in these specific mansions. (11)

---

### The Lineage of the Cosmos

The question arises: what is the origin of these influences? According to the scholar Hema, it is rooted in the thirteen wives of the sage **Kashyapa**, as described in the Geography of the Universe <note>original: *bhūgola*</note>. These thirteen wives are:

1.  **Aditi** <note>mother of the gods</note>
2.  **Diti** <note>mother of the Daityas/demons</note>
3.  **Danu**
4.  **Tamra** <note>mother of birds</note>
5.  **Bhasu**
6.  **Vinata** <note>mother of Garuda</note>
7.  **Surabhi** <note>mother of cattle</note>
8.  **Suprabha**
9.  **Khaganetra**
10. **Mithuna Devi**
11. **Kalindi**
12. **Kanakarekha**
13. **Kanakaprabha**

Through these thirteen wives, the different directions and orientations of the stars—whether facing upward, downward, or sideways—achieve their power <note>original: *siddhi*</note>. This allows for the certain determination of success for all worldly affairs <note>original: *savāsavārtha-nishcayā*</note>. 

Regarding the **Upward-facing stars** <note>original: *ūrdhvamukha*</note>: these include Rohini and others associated with the deity Varuna <note>the god of the oceans and cosmic order</note>. These stars are considered "upward" because of their rising nature and are suitable for activities like building temples or planting trees. (22)

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the Nakshatras (lunar mansions) and their presiding deities. Now, using the **Upajati** meter <note>a classical Sanskrit poetic rhythm</note>, the author speaks of the category known as **Kulodaya** <note>literally "the rising of the lineage," referring to stars that are considered beneficial for family or communal matters</note>. The "mixed" stars <note>original: *mishrai*, referring to the Nakshatras Krittika and Vishakha</note>, the learned say, belong to the assembly of those who possess knowledge of the medicinal arts.

**Mrigashira** <note>the 5th lunar mansion, "the Antelope’s Head"</note>, the "elder-born" <note>original: *agraja*</note>, and the mansion presided over by **Vishwakarma** <note>the divine architect; this refers to the mansion Chitra</note>—these two are the ornamental stars of this group. What are the characteristics of these "mixed" and other stars? They are associated with the "womb" or origin. **Purva Phalguni** <note>the 11th lunar mansion</note> and **Mula** <note>the 19th lunar mansion, "the Root"</note> are joined here. This grouping is not considered troublesome but rather brings happiness and awakening. **Uttara Phalguni**, **Uttara Ashadha**, and **Uttara Bhadrapada** are the "holders" <note>original: *grahini*</note> of this lineage. These thirteen are known as the **Kulodaya** mansions. (24)

Now, again in the **Upajati** meter, he speaks of the **Upakula** and **Kulakula** groups:

The wise say that the mansions beginning with **Karka** <note>referring to a specific starting point in the zodiacal calculation</note> are known as **Upakula** <note>sub-lineage stars</note>. How so?

---

The mixed ones, the medicinal ones, the elder-born, and the mansion of **Vishwakarma** <note>Chitra</note>—these are the portions. There, joined with the two **Ashvins** <note>the twin physicians of the gods, presiding over Ashvini</note>, they are called **Kulodaya**. (24) The stars of the sun-god **Aditya** <note>Punarvasu</note> are said to be of two kinds. The **Upakula** mansions are those associated with the serpent-spirits <note>original: *vyala*, referring to Ashlesha</note>. These are the "Mixed-Lineage" <note>original: *kulakula*</note> stars. (26)

---

The Wind is **Swati**. The Lord of Death is **Bharani**. The Sun’s mother <note>Aditi</note> is **Punarvasu**. The two waters are **Purva Ashadha**. The Sun itself resides in **Hasta**. **Revati** is also among these. These are the mansions known as **Upakula**.

Furthermore, the wise say that **Jyeshtha** <note>the 18th mansion, "the Eldest"</note> combined with the others forms the **Kulakula** group. **Rudra** <note>the storm god</note> is **Ardra**. **Pushya** is associated with the expansion of wealth. The "Vasudevas" <note>the gods of light</note> preside over **Shravana**. The "Unborn-Foot" <note>original: *ajapada*</note> refers to **Purva Bhadrapada**. The "Serpent" <note>original: *vyala*</note> is **Ashlesha**. The Lord of the Waters <note>Varuna</note> rules **Shatabhisha**. The "Friend" <note>original: *mitra*</note> is **Anuradha**. In the science of light <note>original: *jyotishi*, or astrology</note>, these mansions are called **Kulakula**. These are their names as declared until the end of the description. These comprise the twenty-seven divisions <note>original: *kosha*</note> of the stars. (26)

Speaking of the classification beginning with the "Radiance of the Planets," the author uses the term **Eyeless** <note>original: *niraiva*, meaning a star with no sight or "blind"</note> to indicate that in such a state, there is no comfort or success to be found. In this sequence of three, he speaks of the **Pupil-less** <note>original: *vikaninika*, from *kaninika* (pupil of the eye)</note>, where the star is deprived of its central vision. From that, one may become "one-eyed" or "blind" in effect. Then comes the **Union-Seat** <note>original: *yogapitha*</note>, where there is pain at the corners of the eyes. This is followed by the **Troubled-Eye** <note>original: *kalovaka*, likely referring to squinting or distorted vision</note>. These are the "daily eyes" of the stars. In a specific sense, this does not require speculation; the sequence moves from the **Clear-eyed** <note>original: *sulochana*</note> to the **Two-eyed**. On such days, what is lost is truly gone. The commentary states that according to the Shastras <note>sacred scientific treatises</note>, there is a dispute here: the meaning is that under a "Gone-eye" mansion, one's own wealth or property shall not be regained.

Regarding the **Pupil-less** state: if an item is lost then, it is not recovered. In the **Troubled-Eye** mansion, there may be news or talk of the item in the village, but recovery is not achieved. In "Cruel" works, one uses the **Cruel** and **Harsh** mansions—those that are fierce and sharp. Furthermore, the mansions other than those mentioned are for "Well-desired" or auspicious works. Again, in the **Clouded Sign of Action** <note>original: *avila-karma-rashi*, referring to complex or impure tasks</note>, one should undertake the appropriate activities on the designated day.

He describes the greatness of the merits <note>original: *guna-dosha*, referring to the balance of qualities and faults</note>, stating that it "nourishes" <note>original: *pushyati*, the etymological root of the name Pushya</note>. For the people, it is the best of things; it possesses the capacity and power to bring forth success from that which is hidden or distant. What is this power? It is **Pushya**, characterized not merely by one jewel, but by many. It is constructed to ward off faults and fulfill desires. How is this achieved? Through the effort and undertaking <note>original: *arambha*, the beginning of a task</note> initiated in the heavens. Those well-performed deeds <term>Sukarma</term> <note>good or auspicious actions that yield positive karma</note> are known to arise from this source. Just as one might pull a treasure from the ocean, so too does one perceive the complete collection of jewels in this place. It is the most excellent resting place for the flowers of the **Kali** age <note>the current historical age in Hindu cosmology, often considered one of spiritual decline</note>. How is it described? As before, even though the **Kali** age possesses many faults, **Pushya** remains excessively brilliant and full of all prosperity. It leads a multitude of jewels, even those obscured by many faults, and constantly nourishes them. This "Nourisher" <note>original: *Pushya*</note> acts in all rituals and deeds without ceasing.

-> Station 3 <-

The jewel that transforms one's state also performs the "Dance of Pushya" <note>original: *Pushya-nritta*, likely a metaphor for the star's auspicious movement or influence</note>, which brings about auspiciousness. Thus, seeing what has been done in the world, one should speak of the excellence of this mansion. The term **Nishpa** <note>original: *nishpa*, meaning accomplished or certain</note> has many meanings here, much like the moon-like **Pushya**. In the practice of domestic rituals, one observes the influence of one's birth; in that context—

—it is certain that **Pushya** nourishes. It performs the act of nourishing and accomplishes the tasks that have been undertaken. # The Wheel of Calamitous Combinations

Now, the author describes the **Wheel of Omens and Adversarial Combinations** <note>original: *Utpāta-ari-yoga-cakra*</note>. Regarding the planets that move through the celestial sphere, the calculation for all the planets' timing is done using the cycle of the **Dual-Deity Star** <note>original: *Dvidaiva*, referring to the lunar mansion **Viśākhā**, which is presided over by the two gods Indra and Agni</note>. By counting the lunar mansions <note>original: *nakshatra*</note> in the wheel, according to the proper sequence, the following combinations <term>yogas</term> are produced: 1. **Kāla** <term>Time/Death</term>, 2. **Kāla**, and 3. **Saumya** <term>Gentle or Auspicious</term>. These yield results according to their specific natures. 

For instance, if it is Sunday <note>original: *Arkadi*</note> and the current star is **Viśākhā**, then the yoga is determined. Here, the first **Kāla** is considered "silver" <note>indicating a medium intensity of the omen</note>, the second **Kāla** is "golden" <note>indicating the most severe or intense timing</note>, and the **Saumya** is "white" or "bright" <note>indicating a favorable outcome</note>. In this wheel, these combinations occur in a specific order. Counting from the first star, **Vaiśākha** <note>Viśākhā</note>, through to **Pūrvāṣāḍhā**, there are 34 divisions. This is explained in the following verses set in the *Vaitālīya* poetic meter, which describes the timing of these combinations: 

Starting from the star of the **Ancestors** <note>original: *Pitṛ*, referring to the lunar mansion **Maghā**</note> and the **Serpent** <note>original: *Ahi*, referring to the lunar mansion **Āśleṣā**</note>, one calculates the positions. Just as the Sun moves through the sky, one considers the mansion of the **Ancestors** and the dual-deity star **Viśākhā**. When Mars <note>original: *Bhauma*</note> and Saturn <note>original: *Sani*</note> align in these positions, the results are as follows:

-> In the wheel of the Dual-Deity stars, the combinations appear in sequence. <-
-> For the preceding planets, these are known as the Omens of Time (*Utpāta-kāla*). <-
-> These names reflect their true nature and reveal the influence of the day. <-
-> From the Ancestors' star to the Serpent's, the divine influence is measured. <-

The influence continues through the star of **Fortune** <note>original: *Bhagya*, referring to **Pūrvaphālgunī**</note> and the star of **Venus** <note>original: *Bhārgava*</note>. If a combination falls under the influence of the **Lord of the Sky** <note>original: *Nabhame*, likely referring to the Sun or a specific zenith point</note>, it is known as the **Ceya** yoga. This is calculated with precision using the positions of the **Serpents** <note>original: *Bhujaga*</note> and the establishment of the celestial order.

# The Boat Diagram

Next, the **Boat Diagram** <term>Nauraka</term> <note>A specialized astrological chart used to determine safety during travel or the success of new ventures</note> is described. This involves the positions of **Brahmā** <note>original: *Viriñci*</note> and **Viṣṇu** <note>original: *Upendra*</note>, and the influence of the **Outsiders** <note>original: *Mleccha*</note>. When the stars are crossed by these influences, one should not undertake a journey. On such a day, the dreams one has of the **Lord** <note>original: *Bhagavat*</note> may be troubled. 

Under the influence of Venus <note>original: *Bhārgava/Śukra*</note> or Jupiter <note>original: *Guru*</note>, certain actions like the marriage of a pregnant woman or the installation of a deity should be avoided if the stars are in an "extinguished" <note>original: *asta*, referring to heliacal setting or planetary combustion</note> state. For Saturn <note>original: *Śani*</note>, if the star is extinguished, it is always considered a **Bhīṣa** yoga <term>Terrifying Combination</term>. Sages say that for births, deaths, or departures, one must look to the "hand" <note>a specific division of the chart</note> of the planet. If the diagram shows the "Serpent King" <note>original: *Bhujagaguru*</note> holding the hand, or if it falls in the divisions of the gods, it signifies the destruction of one's efforts. Therefore, one must always remember the ritual rules of these divisions to avoid misfortune.

# The Combination of the Orbs

Now, the author describes the **Combination of the Orbs** <note>original: *Maṇḍalayoga*</note>. It is said that seven factors exist toward the north. Their divisions are determined by seven measures of strength. There are further divisions based on the sixteen **Kings** <note>original: *nṛpālakai*</note>, the fourteen **Manus** <note>progenitors of humanity in Hindu cosmology; here representing the number 14</note>, the twenty-one **Yamas** <note>restraints or gods of death; here representing the number 21</note>, the twenty-two **Twin Beauties** <note>original: *ramāśvī*; a poetic way to indicate the number 22</note>, and the twenty-three **Sages** <note>original: *ṛṣibhis*; referring to the Saptarishi or enlightened seers</note>. Measured by these rays, the divisions of the orbs are determined. **[41]** Now, he speaks of the results of these:

-> Through these divisions and measures, through the nine guardians of the circle, <-
-> through the fifteen, through the fourteen Manus, the twenty-one Yamas, <-
-> the twenty-two, and the twenty-three, twenty-four orbs are determined. <-
-> These result in the **rain of strength** <note>or rain of the army</note>, the falling of hail, <-
-> and the destruction of actions within the circle. These are declared to be <-
-> unfavorable for ritual actions, for sleeping, or for the gathering of armies. **[42]** <-

By the "wise ones," the result of **mobilizing the army** <term>sainya-karṣaṇa</term> is explained. The term "water" refers to various sources such as ponds, **wells, and gardens** <note>original: *kūpārāmadika*</note>. "Stone" <note>original: *upala*</note> refers to rocks or masonry. Each of these is considered individually in combination. One must understand the flow of actions, the methods of piercing, and the origins of **fortifications** <note>original: *durga*; referring to forts or strongholds</note>. These combinations are said to be disregarded or avoided <note>original: *tiraskṛtā*</note> when they produce many faults or impurities in the ritual site.

**Venus** <note>original: *Śukraḥ*</note> is the hand itself, meaning the "lotus hand." Its **mallet** <note>original: *mogaraḥ*; a heavy wooden hammer or club</note> is held in the hand. When performing actions such as the construction of **dams or bridges** <note>original: *seturādika*</note>, the mobilization of forces, or the binding of things, the action becomes **subject to faults** <term>kriyā-doṣa-bhāg</term>. These actions do not bear fruit or remain unstable, as if they were sinking into the mud. This is the conclusion of the sages. **[43]** 

Now, he describes the **Vidula** <note>a technical term for a specific division of a lunar mansion or a particular rhythmic interval in time</note>. The Vidula is said to be formed by the "rays" belonging to the Sun and the Moon. Through the connection with the Sun, it enters the **Vidula** state. The calculation of the Vidula is as follows:

-> The Vidula is nectar and provides a touch of strength, <-
-> Nourishing the body and providing sustenance. <-
-> When measured by the count of six and six, <-
-> That is what the Vidula is known to be. **[44]**

In the field of astrology <note>original: *Jyotiśca*</note>, when the moon is present in a particular **Lunar Mansion** <term>nakṣatra</term>, one should take that foundation and add seven. By dividing the sum of the mansions and the "rays" <note>original: *bhānām*</note> by seven, the **remainder** <term>śeṣa</term> reveals the result. If the calculation results in the "body-nourishing" remainder, the Vidula becomes effective. However, if there is a specific remainder known as the "arrow" <note>original: *iṣu*</note>, it causes destruction. It is said that such a Vidula **destroys and annihilates** <note>original: *vināśayati*</note> the fruits of the lunar mansion. **[44]**

# Now, the Combinations for Lightning, Trembling, and Other Phenomena

By taking the rays of the **Enemy of Darkness** <note>original: *timirāri*; a poetic name for the Sun</note> and covering them <unclear>with the teeth</unclear>, when measured by **five units**, the combination for **lightning** <term>vidyut</term> occurs. In this same way, if measured by **seven units**, the combination for an **earthquake** <term>bhūkampa</term> occurs. With two measures, it is known as a "shaker." With **ten units** appearing in equal measure, the combination for **Saturn** <note>original: *Śani-yoga*</note> occurs.

> The rays of the Sun <note>Enemy of Darkness</note> are 5;
> For the trembling of the earth, they are 7.
> In the same measure of 7,
> Saturn itself appears at 45.
> For the planet **Ketu** <note>the descending lunar node</note>, the mansions are 18.
> For the **Lunar Day** <term>tithi</term>, the measure is 15.
> For the **Staff** <note>original: *daṇḍaka*; a specific astrological configuration</note> in the mansion of the owl,
> The wandering mansions are 19,
> And for the **Thunderbolt** <note>original: *aśani*; also meaning a flash of lightning</note>, the eyes are 24.
> The turning points of the era are 25 and 48.

It shall be 45. Here, for the **descending node** <note>original: *ketu*</note>, the planets or mansions are **eighteen**. For the **Staff** <term>daṇḍaka</term>, the lunar days are **fifteen**. For the "wanderers," the mansions are **nineteen**.

<note>This text uses a system of numerology common in medieval Indian astronomy where specific natural phenomena are mapped to numerical remainders (measured units) calculated from the positions of the Sun and Moon. The "Staff" and "Thunderbolt" likely refer to specific omens or portents within the *Saṃhitā* tradition of astrology.</note>
