# The Malefic Turning of the Wheel of Time

Now, regarding the **Turning of the Wheel of Time** <term>Kālacakrabhrama</term> <note>a specific astrological defect where the "gears" of time are said to turn against the success of an undertaking</note> in the **Tiger's Play** meter <term>Śārdūlavikrīḍita</term> <note>a complex 19-syllable Sanskrit poetic meter often used for authoritative or descriptive verses</note> beginning with the word **Heli** <note>original: *heli*; a Sanskrit term for the Sun derived from the Greek *helios*</note>. In this verse, "Heli" refers to the Sun. When combined with the **constellations** <term>nakshatra</term> present at the **setting of the Sun and Moon**, if they are in a state of "mixing," the **Lord Mars** <note>original: *Maṅgala-bhagavān*; Mars is personified as a deity associated with heat, war, and energy</note> brings about the Turning of the Wheel of Time, which causes the **destruction of success** in disputes and other such activities.

In the first instance, the Moon is the lord of the **night** <note>original: *vibhāvarī*</note>. Mars is the **son of the Earth** <note>original: *dharābhū*</note>. When these two are placed in **fierce constellations** <note>original: *ugre-bhe*; a category of constellations including Magha and Bharani, considered harsh in nature</note>, or when the sons of the Sun and Mercury <note>Saturn and Mercury</note> are in **friendly signs** <note>original: *maitre-bhe*</note>, or when the **Son of the Sun** <note>Saturn</note> and Mercury are in **mixed constellations** <note>original: *miśra-bhe*; such as Vishakha or Krittika</note>, or again when the lords of the constellations, **Venus and the Moon**, are in friendly signs...

---

->**The Sun and the Moon are set, and the Son of Earth**<-
->**Is in fierce signs; Mercury and Saturn are in mixed or friendly signs;**<-
->**Lord Mars, appearing fierce like lightning in the middle of the night,**<-
->**Causes the entire Wheel of Time to turn inauspiciously. 48**<-

---

The phrase **darkness of the night** <note>original: *niśīthinī-pāṃśu*</note> refers to the period where the light is obscured and terrifying. When these planets are in such a state, the Turning of the Wheel occurs. Here, the term for the Moon's lordship is used to show the relationship between the two celestial bodies. Regarding the word for **night** <note>original: *niśīthinī*</note>, it is noted that there is a long "i" sound in the middle of the "sh" character; however, variations in spelling and pronunciation are observed in different texts <note>original: *śabda-prabhedā dṛśyante*; a philological note regarding the orthography of the manuscript</note>. 48.

# The Descent Beginning with the Moon

Now, he speaks of the **Descent Beginning with the Moon** <term>Candrādyupāta</term> <note>a specific astrological point of "falling" or descent that indicates a period of malefic influence</note>. In the verse beginning with the word **Candra** <note>original: *Candra*; the Moon</note>, the calculation involves the Sun and the Moon. By dividing the degrees of the Sun and Moon, one determines the position of the **Ascendant** <term>Lagna</term>. From there, one counts through the various signs and degrees to find the specific planetary influence. This sequence involves the deities and the **Brahmin sages** <term>Vipra</term> <note>priests or scholars who maintain the sacred knowledge of the stars</note> such as **Bhrigu** <note>original: *Bhrigu-deva*; the sage associated with the planet Venus</note>.

When the planets are combined and joined in this manner, it affects the "receptacle" or the base of the calculation. This involves the **Seven Planets** <term>Saptagraha</term>. Just as **Gauri** <note>a name for the goddess Parvati</note> is the daughter of the **Himalayas** <note>original: *Himācalatā*; personified as the king of mountains</note>, this calculation arises from the "rotation" of the celestial bodies. 

<margin>20</margin>
The following is the connection: the first descent belongs to the Moon, and from that **Node** <term>Pāta</term> <note>an astronomical point where orbits intersect, often considered spiritually significant or dangerous</note>, the various other descents are calculated. This is clarified in the verse below.

<margin>The work called "The Beautiful Turning" should be performed during the ritual of the constellations. 41</margin>

-> The Moon's fruit is divided by the Sun; from the knowledge of **Vishakha**, **Anuradha**, and **Ashvini**, <-
-> and from **Revati** <note>original: *Pauṣṇa*; the constellation Revati, whose presiding deity is Puṣan</note>, the sequence follows. <-
-> From the counts of the gods, humans, and the ocean, let the wise identify <-
-> the **Descent of the Constellations** in the work named **The Beautiful Turning**. 41 <-

One should establish all the constellations starting from the constellation occupied by the Sun. These include **Vishakha**, **Anuradha**, **Ashvini**, and **Revati**. If the current constellation at the time of an event matches these specific points in the calculation relative to the Sun's position, then that moment is known as the **Malefic Descent** <term>Upapāta</term>. The wise and those learned in the stars call this the beginning of "The Beautiful Turning" <term>Vakruchiram</term> <note>the name of this specific astrological yoga or configuration</note>.

<vocab>ज्योतिष (Jyotisha): Astrology/Astronomy. नक्षत्र (Nakshatra): Lunar mansion or constellation. चन्द्राद्युपात (Chandradyupata): A specific malefic point calculated from the Moon. सूर्य (Surya): The Sun. चन्द्र (Chandra): The Moon. पात (Pata): A node or "fall." हिमाचलता गोरी (Himachalata Gauri): Gauri, daughter of the Himalayas. भकर्म्मणि (Bhakarmmani): In the ritual or work of the constellations.</vocab>

### The Intersection of Celestial Light

Now, just as those lines are perceived by a person, when at a certain time the two **"flowering ones"** <note>original: *pushpavantau*; a poetic reference to the Sun and Moon, who "bloom" in the sky</note> are positioned so that their lines intersect, an **Intersection of Light** <term>Tejah-sampata</term> <note>A point where the rays or astrological influences of the Sun and Moon cross</note> occurs. From that union, because of the fires, a "cruel-angled" shape is formed. These alignments are always the primary causes for the **Destruction of Auspiciousness** <term>Mangala-bhanga</term> and the destruction of the planetary fruits. They act like various weapons or sharp needles <unclear>khivarabhi</unclear> that descend from the surface of the sky, moving toward the ocean. 1.

When the intersection of the gaze of the Sun and Moon occurs, it produces a terrifying light. At that time, men on the surface of the earth experience the causes of the destruction of great auspiciousness. 51. Truly, this "strike" or "flaw" is what turns an auspicious moment into an inauspicious one. Even for the **Skull-bearer** <term>Kapalin</term> <note>An epithet of the god Shiva, referring to his ascetic form carrying a skull</note>, was there not a flaw in his auspiciousness due to the **Fault of Conjunction** <term>Pata-dosha</term>? 53.

Thus is the calculation. 61. Now, he explains the fault from a different perspective, beginning with "Truth." Your breath and fame is **Shiva** <note>original: *Shambhu*</note>, and she is **Parvati** <note>original: *Gauri*</note>, the one who dwells in the heart-lotus. As it was said in ancient times, when the marriage—the **Taking of the Hand** <term>Panigrahana</term>—of Parvati and Shiva took place, it was the height of auspiciousness. Yet, O Blessed One, if even for the "Skull-bearer" Shiva, the marriage became a source of this conjunction-flaw, then how much more so for others?

### The Sequence of the Fixed Half-Lunar Days

Now, he describes the sequence relating to the fixed **half-lunar days** <term>Karana</term> <note>A Karana is half of a Tithi (lunar day); there are 11 types of Karanas which rotate through the lunar month</note>. Near the end of the month, during the latter half of the New Moon <note>original: *Amavasya*</note> and the preceding days, the sequence is explained. In the latter half of the **fourteenth lunar day** <note>original: *Chaturdashi*</note> of the dark fortnight, the fixed sequence begins. From that fourteenth day onward, the three movable <insert>and then fixed</insert> Karanas, starting with **Shakuni**, come into being.

1. Now, regarding the calculation of the Karanas starting from the bright fortnight: starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should determine the accumulated Karanas. What is the meaning? When a certain number of lunar days have passed, what is the resulting accumulation?

In this way, during the dark fortnight, starting from the fourteenth day, the fixed Karanas—**Shakuni**, **Chatushpada**, **Naga**, and **Kimstughna**—occur in succession. 1. From the start of the bright fortnight, the calculation of the Karana is made by taking the number of elapsed lunar days, doubling them, and then <unclear>calculating</unclear> the sum. Aside from these specific fixed Karanas, the others are considered **movable** <term>Chara</term> <note>Movable Karanas like Bava and Balava repeat in a cycle, whereas the four fixed ones occur only once per lunar month</note>. These are used by the wise for the successful completion of gentle or auspicious deeds.

That sum, decreased by one—for what purpose? It is then divided by the appropriate number, and the remainder indicates the specific Karana reached, such as **Bava** and the others. 1. Now, he speaks of the fruits or results of this knowledge. The **movable** Karanas are for the **attainment of success in all auspicious works** <note>original: *subhasamasta-karyasiddhi*</note>. Similarly, the wise use the **fixed** Karanas, such as **Shakuni**, specifically for **nourishing or strengthening rituals** <term>Paustika</term> <note>Rituals intended to increase wealth, health, or well-being</note>. Furthermore, the movable Karanas should be utilized in the performance of **marriage ceremonies** <note>original: *vivahadi-vidhau*</note> and other such rites. 4.

### The Division of the Limbs of Bhadra

**Now he describes the division of her limbs, etc., beginning with the word "Nija" [her own].** Regarding this, it is known that for Bhadra, who is born [from the lunar day], her own body is divided into portions. The sixth part <note>Original: "Shadamshakah."</note> consists of five **Ghatis** <term>Ghati</term> <note>A unit of 24 minutes.</note>; this is the mouth or face <note>Original: "Lapan-vadana."</note>. Thus, out of thirty parts, the [next] portion is the throat or neck. Then follows the eighth portion, and the tenth portion is the chest or the heart. The front part [is the heart]. The sixth part—five **Ghatis**—is the navel. Then follows the fifth portion, and the sixth part is called the waist <note>Original: "Kati."</note>. The three-measured short part is the creeping tail <note>Original: "Langula-latta," literally the tail-stroke or tail-vine.</note>. || 15 ||

> ->Her own six parts [5 Ghatis] are the mouth; [then] the throat;<-
> ->the chest portion is designated as eleven; the navel as five;<-
> ->the waist is stated as six; and the tail-vine is known as three.<- 
> ->This division of her body is thus spoken of by me as thirty-six [or thirty] units,<-
> ->explained through reasoning for the sake of those who bow [to knowledge].<-
> ->This has been stated by me according to the tradition. || 16 ||<-

**Now he speaks of the discrimination of the parts when Bhadra is shorter or longer [than the standard duration].** By the word "Maya" [by me], it is meant that for those Brahmins <note>Original: "Vipra."</note> or wise ones who are joined with this method, this is always the rule. The division of the five-fold limbs of Bhadra has been declared and told. For this reason, in the calculation of a residence <note>Original: "Sadma-vidhi," likely referring to house-building or auspicious placement.</note>, this division should be considered and accepted by the wise. What is meant by this? When the duration of Bhadra is longer [than the standard 30 Ghatis], the division of the parts should be adjusted proportionally <note>Original: "Sadrisho bhavet," meaning the parts should remain similar or in the same ratio.</note>. 17

### Rules regarding the Upendravajra Meter

Now, in the **Upendravajra meter** <note>original: *Upendravajrā*; a Sanskrit poetic meter consisting of 11 syllables per line</note>, the text describes the descent of the eclipse. For as long as the celestial bodies are obscured, the "dwellers of heaven" <note>original: *divaukaso*; referring to the deities or the Sun and Moon themselves</note> are considered to be in a state of distress. This state lasts for a period of **four watches** <term>Yama|A traditional unit of time lasting approximately three hours; four watches equal twelve hours or half a day</term>. During the eclipses of the Sun and the Moon, which occur at the lunar junctures <term>Parva|The transition points of the new or full moon</term>, certain faults arise. Until the eclipse has fully passed, one should remain focused on the recitation of protective **mantras** <note>sacred chants</note> in those specific locations. 1.

Furthermore, regarding the "obstructions" <note>original: *antarayāṇi*</note> that arise during the eclipse process... <unclear>rallamallm</unclear>... these are considered inauspicious for five types of actions. 5.

### Rules regarding the Upajātī Meter

Now, in the **Upajātī meter** <note>original: *Upajātī*; a common Sanskrit meter that combines elements of Indravajrā and Upendravajrā</note>, he explains the faults related to the "Lord of Shadows" <note>referring to Rahu</note>. When the eclipse juncture occurs, for as long as the celestial bodies are transiting, the four watches of the deities remain in effect. If an eclipse is... <unclear>cheya-graha</unclear>... 11. In the case of those inauspicious moments, which are five-fold, if the eclipse is **Total** <note>original: *kṛtsne*; meaning the entire disk of the Sun or Moon is covered</note>, or if it is merely a **Fragment** <note>original: *śakala*; a partial eclipse</note>, the duration of restricted activity is calculated by groups of days. These are measured as **seven days** <note>original: *nangaiḥ*; a numerical code where "mountains" or "limbs" often represent the number seven</note>, **five days** <note>5</note>, or other counts of days depending on the magnitude of the eclipse. 6.

### Determining the Period of Avoidance

The distinction regarding the "greater eclipse" is as follows: In the case of a **total eclipse** <note>original: *kṛtsne sampūrṇa grahaṇe*</note>, the wise should set aside **seven days** as inauspicious. One must avoid performing any **auspicious deeds** <term>Subha-kṛtya|Religious ceremonies, marriages, or important new beginnings</term> during this time. 

Following this order:
*   For a total eclipse: **7 days** of avoidance.
*   For an eclipse where more than half is obscured: **5 days**.
*   For a partial eclipse <note>original: *śakale*</note>: **4 days**.
*   For an eclipse where only a small portion is touched: **3 days**.

This is the clear explanation <note>original: *spaṣṭaṃ*</note> of the duration of the impact. 6. 8.

### On the Influence of Consumed Planets

Now, concerning the state of being **singularly consumed** <note>original: *ekāntam-abhukta*; refers to a planet being entirely eclipsed or overshadowed by another's influence</note>. At that time, through the influence of the planets upon **Mars** <term>Mangala|The planet associated with energy and the commander of the celestial assembly</term>, the timing of **marriages** <note>original: *vivāha*</note> is considered. Is there anything specific regarding the constellation? It is as if the time has passed being "consumed by the ocean" <note>original: *sāgareṇa bhuktaṃ*; 'ocean' often symbolically represents the number four in Sanskrit numerology, or suggests a vast, overwhelming influence</note>. 

Furthermore, this applies to the current time of the transit, the time immediately approaching the transit, or when the planet is **pierced** <term>Viddha|An astrological phenomenon where the influence of one planet or point is obstructed or 'wounded' by the presence of another</term> at the end of a specific period. This also includes when a planet is situated in its own **battle** <note>original: *saṃgrāma*; planetary combat occurs when two planets are in close conjunction, usually within one degree</note>, or when there is a division between its current position and its highest point of exaltation.

When **Venus** <term>Shukra|The planet of beauty, love, and the teacher of the demons</term> is consumed or joined with such an influence, or when it is separated from its own exaltation, its power is diminished. If these planets are not in their proper positions, then the auspiciousness of the marriage is affected. In such cases, one must follow the sequence of the planets. Again, regarding a **group of six months** <note>original: *māsa ṣat-kaṃ*; a specific half-year period</note>, the planetary conjunction <term>Graha Yoga|The alignment or union of planets</term> must be observed for twenty-three intervals. 8.

Alternatively, according to the established doctrine regarding those two planets, there is a calculation for the slowing of the two bodies. When influenced by **malefic planets** <term>Krura|Literally 'cruel' or 'harsh' planets, such as Mars, Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu</term>, a malefic state is reached. In this singular state, when "pierced" by a malefic influence, the planets are separated. 

Some teachers <note>original: *ācāryā*; the ancient authorities on astronomical science</note> maintain that a **six-month planetary conjunction** creates a specific result. When this yoga <note>alignment</note> is attained, one must consider the protection of the time and the removal of the "anger" or harshness of the transition.

### On the Latitudinal Portions 

Now, regarding the portions of the arrows of the mansions <term>bhasāyaka-lavānām|The degrees of celestial latitude (śara) associated with the stars</term>: with eleven, in the **Northern direction** <note>original: "saumya"</note>, it is always **seven** <insert>7</insert>. From the beginning of the "Fire-mansion" <note>the nakshatra Krittika</note>, in the dance of the calculations, the **portions of the arrows** <note>original: "vāṇalava"; units of 5</note> are frequently established for the conjunctions of Yama <note>Bharani</note> and the Wise One <note>Mercury or a specific star</note>.

The clarified fixed positions are: **The Senses and the Twins** <note>original: "indriyāśvinaḥ"; Senses (5) and Twins (2) indicating 25</note>; the **Worlds, the Mountains, and the Arrows** <note>original: "śarādrilokaḥ"; Arrows (5), Mountains (7), and Worlds (3) indicating 375</note>; the **Excellent Oceans and the Twins** <note>24 or 27</note>. The sequence of the **Fixed Degrees** <term>dhruvakāṃśakāḥ|Longitudinal coordinates measured along the ecliptic</term> follows: Sky (0), Flavors (6), Principles (25), Qualities (3), Mountains (7), and Immortals (3). These start from the first mansion <note>Ashvini</note> in order: **21**.

The directions are defined as **Northern** <note>original: "saumya"</note> and **Southern** <note>original: "dakṣiṇa"</note>. The **Arrow-faced** <note>original: "śilīmukhā"; a synonym for arrows, representing the number 5</note> and the **Skull-bearer** <note>original: "kapālinaḥ"; representing the number 11, referring to the 11 Rudras</note>. The movement of the sun’s path <term>ayana|The northward or southward course of the sun</term> is categorized by these five speeds.

The clarified calculation is declared: **Northern** refers to the **North direction**. In these directions, ten portions of the arrows <note>5</note> are found. The **Earth-Arrows** <note>original: "ku-viśikhā-vāṇāḥ"</note> are **five** <insert>2</insert>. The **Southern** refers to the **South direction**. The **Arrow-faced** are **five**. If one asks how the **Sky-Movers** <term>khecara|Planets</term> traveling in the northern and mid-regions are to be understood in their course, the answer is given: that which is in the south... with the eastern atmosphere... following the **Prime Meridian** <term>rekhā|The longitudinal line used as a reference point, often passing through Ujjain</term>. 

Now, he describes the positions of the stars in different celestial circles. The **True Position** <term>sphuṭa|The "corrected" or actual observed position of a planet</term> is determined by the **Southern Latitude** <term>śara|Literally 'arrow'; in astronomy, it refers to celestial latitude</term>. A planet is "True" or clear when it is **With-Arrow** <note>original: "seṣu"; refers to a planet possessing celestial latitude</note>. A planet that is **Without-Arrow** <note>original: "vinyo-nabhaścara"; a planet at zero latitude</note> is equal to a planet at the celestial equator. At that time, that planet—within the circle of the stars marked with the characteristics described by the God of the Astrological Wheel—has a different threefold expansion. It becomes radiant, and through that star, it is said to be "enveloped." This is the meaning. <note>24</note> 

Now, regarding the **Planetary Seizures** <note>original: "grahaṇā"; eclipses or occultations</note>:

When a planet is **With-Arrow** <note>possessing latitude</note>, then by that "with-arrow" sky-mover, it becomes equal to the circle of the stars. The experts say it is then "pervaded" by its power. <note>25</note> A **Conjunction** <term>samāgama|A meeting or union of two celestial bodies</term> occurs when there is a pleasant union between the two in a peaceful state. Through the **Friction of Stars** <term>vimarda|Total occultation or a 'clash' where one body covers another</term>, a **Grazing** <term>ullekhana|A conjunction where the orbs of the planets appear to touch or scrape</term> or a **Splitting** <term>bheda|An occultation where one body appears to pierce through the other</term> of the brilliance occurs, depending on the distinction of their light. <note>26</note>

### Chapter on the Conjunction of Stars
<note>original: "Nakṣatra-saṅgamādhikāra"</note>

He explains the **Chapter on the Conjunction of Stars**, beginning with "Sama" (Equal). When there is a "Superior Interval" between two celestial bodies staying within the mansions, and there is a mutual "Good Union" <note>original: "su-yoga"</note>—that is, a union of their light rays—a **Meeting** <term>samāgama|Conjunction</term> occurs. 

From the stars' mutual friction or clash, a union of the planet and star occurs. If, at the time of this friction, the number of rays is high, it becomes a **War** <term>yuddha|Planetary war; a very close conjunction where planets seem to compete in brilliance</term>. Furthermore, when joined with the Sun, or when two stars are joined, a **Grazing** <note>original: "ullekhana"</note> occurs between them. From their distinct piercing, a **Splitting of Brilliance** <note>original: "bheda-dyuti"</note> occurs. <note>26</note>

## The Timing of Planetary Influences

Now, regarding the cessation of the rising of these stars and planets, and the nature of the **Sky-Movers** <term>khecara|Planets</term> and the **Lunar Mansions** <term>nakṣatra|The 27 star clusters of the Hindu zodiac</term>. When two planets are supported by a conjunction in two different signs, one should examine the results. If they are auspicious and favorable, their influence in the villages and lands may last for up to six months. Through a partial conjunction, the effects are experienced again at the root of those planets. 

Regarding business and auspicious marriage rites: if the activity is performed when the planets are moving toward completion, the results manifest within three to seven years, or sometimes within three months. For auspicious works, there is an arrival of success. In conflict or war, if one remains steady until the cessation of the influence, victory is achieved through the second position. <note>27</note>

## Mutual Positions and Duration

The term **Mutually** <note>original: "parasparam"</note> refers to the relative positions of those planets and stars. When the strength of the rising stars and the two powerful planets is joined in two signs, the auspicious influence remains for six months. This applies to the beginning of a task, or when one is returning from a forest journey. <note>27</note> 

When they are situated mutually, until the end of the message of the stars, and as long as they stay in conjunction for the remaining months, one should complete the intended action within that duration. <note>28</note> Regarding the positions of the **Sun** <term>arka|The Sun</term> and the **Lord of the Night** <term>vibhāvarīśa|The Moon</term>: when there is a union of the Earth and the Moon, and the Sun’s path is reversed, then there is a parity of the declinations.

<gloss>The two nodes and the accomplishment of nourishment. 29</gloss>

In the remaining months of that planetary action, one should finish the work. The star situated in the conjunction of the Sun and Moon at their rising... likewise, one should join the remaining time with the star occupied by a **Cruel Planet** <term>krūra graha|Malefic planets such as Mars or Saturn</term> that stays within the limit. <note>29</note> 

If one asks about the text regarding **Declination Parity** <term>krānti-sāmya|A state where two celestial bodies have the same declination, considered a sensitive astrological point</term>: if the Sun and the Moon—the lords of day and night—are in an equal state or if the Sun's path is in the reverse order of the **True Positions** <term>sphuṭa|Corrected planetary coordinates</term>, then the wise call this occurrence the "Node of Declination Parity." It is said to be a **Sacred Node** <term>parva|A change of phase or a joint in time, often used for eclipses or significant alignments</term>. What is special about this is that it brings the accomplishment of nourishment.

## The Circle of Declination and the Aindra Alignment

Now, regarding the **Circle of Declination** <term>krānticakra|The ecliptic, or the path of the Sun</term> called the *Aindra* [of Indra]. If the Sun and Moon should both be situated upon a single line—specifically when located in the sign of Aries, the month of Chaitra, and the position of Jupiter—then, within the context of the **Circle of Inclination** <term>upakramacakra|A diagnostic circle used to measure the tilt of planetary paths</term>, there occurs a possibility of equality between the two "arms" of the declination circles. This state is known as **Declination Parity** <term>krāntisāmya|A state where two celestial bodies reach the same angular distance from the celestial equator</term>. 

When does this occur? It is said to take place after twenty **Ghatikas** <term>ghati|A traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> have passed in the division of the *Aindra-yoga*. <note>The text indicates "3," likely a marker for a specific subsection or result.</note> Similarly, in the alignment born of the North, when the auspicious division has passed, the teacher instructs that it occurs after forty *Ghatikas*. <note>3</note>

### Now, the Padmaka Festival

See here regarding the **Padmaka** festival: it occurs when the full moon of both **Madhu** <note>original: "madhu"; a poetic name for the month of Chaitra</note> and **Madhava** <note>original: "mādhava"; a poetic name for the month of Vaishakha</note>—specifically the month of **Vaishakha**—falls under a specific condition. What are its characteristics?

It must be joined with the lunar mansion <term>Viśākhā|The 16th nakshatra or lunar mansion in Hindu astrology</term>. Furthermore, what else? It must possess the <term>Vyatipāta|An astronomical yoga or alignment considered extremely powerful for ritual charity</term> alignment. From this, the Sun (2), Saturn, and Jupiter must be aligned. When it occurs alongside the sixth solar day, that is the festival named **Padmaka**. ॥ 39 ॥

### Now, he describes the Kapila-shashthi

Regarding **Nabhasya** <note>original: "nabhasya"; the month of Bhadrapada</note>: the sixth lunar day of the dark half <term>kṛṣṇa-pakṣa|The waning phase of the moon</term> of the month of **Bhadrapada** is known as **Kapila**. 

What are its characteristics? That sixth day <note>original: "ṣaṣṭhī"</note> occurs together with **Ara** <note>original: "āra"; a name for the planet Mars</note> or **Bhauma** <note>Mars</note>. Furthermore, what? It is joined with the **Vyatipata** alignment. Furthermore, what? It occurs when the full moon of **Padmaka** has passed and the day is known as a Wednesday. When the two months of **Madhu** and **Madhava** occur, and the stars are aligned, then the sixth day of the dark half of **Bhadrapada**—joined with **Vyatipata** in the month of **Ashvina**—these are said to be the indicators of the **Kapila** name by the planets. With Mars and the designated weapons <note>original: "āyudhaiḥ"; likely referring to the iconography of the deity or the planetary alignment's sharp influence</note>, the bright light of **Nabhasya** appears. ॥ 40 ॥

The **Amavasya** <note>the New Moon</note>, the **Yugadi** <note>the start of a cosmic age</note>, and the **Manvadi** <note>the start of a reign of a Manu</note> are the limits of the essence of time. Through these, one achieves the accumulation of merit and the destruction of sins... ॥ 41 ॥

When the great lunar mansion **Rohini** <note>the 4th nakshatra, associated with growth and beauty</note> occurs together with the Sun situated in the sign of... occupying the **Ratna** nakshatra. ॥ 5 ॥ 

### Regarding the Ashtaka-shashthi

He speaks of the **Ashtaka-shashthi**: it moves with **Budha** <note>the planet Mercury</note> in the months of **Margashirsha**, **Tapas** <note>the month of Magha</note>, and **Sarasya** <note>the month of Pausha</note>. In **Pausha**, on the sixth day, this is the dark half of **Bhadrapada**, joined with the waning phase among the planets... for **Mangala** <note>Mars</note>, in ceremonies such as marriage, this is desired by the kings. ॥ 50 ॥ 

Now, regarding the **Disham-ati** <note>likely "Diksaṃmati," or the agreement of directions</note>, it becomes known by one's own command. With effort, in the village or home, for twelve days, thus are the dates of the **Yugadi** and other transitions.

Regarding the lunar days <term>Tithis|A lunar day in the Hindu calendar, calculated based on the longitudinal angle between the Sun and Moon</term> calculated from the position of the Sun: the rules for <term>Śrāddha|Ritual offerings made to ancestors</term> are determined by them. ### Now, he describes the Yugadi Lunar Days

Regarding the **Yugadi** <term>Yugādi|The 'beginning of a Yuga'; the specific anniversaries of the start of the four great world ages</term> dates: 

In the **Krita** age <note>The Satya Yuga or Golden Age</note>, it is the ninth lunar day of the bright half <term>śukla-pakṣa|The waxing phase of the moon</term> of the month of **Kartika**. 
In the **Treta** age, it is the third lunar day of the bright half of **Vaishakha** <note>Known as Akshaya Tritiya</note>. 
In the **Dvapara** age, it is the new moon <term>Amāvāsyā|The 15th day of the dark fortnight</term> of the month of **Magha**. 
In the **Kali** age <note>The current age of spiritual decline</note>, it is the thirteenth lunar day of the dark half <term>kṛṣṇa-pakṣa|The waning phase of the moon</term> of **Nabhasya**—that is, the month of **Bhadrapada**. 
These are known as the **Yugadi** dates, the primary lunar days for these eras. ॥ 43 ॥

### Now, he describes the Manvantaras

2. The twelfth lunar day of the bright half of **Kartika**.
3. The third lunar day of the bright half of **Chaitra** <note>original: "madhu"</note>.

9. The eighth lunar day of the dark half of **Bhadrapada** <note>original: "nabhasya"</note>. ॥ 45 ॥

12. The full moon of the bright half of **Phalguna**.
13. The full moon of **Chaitra**.
14. The full moon of **Jyeshtha**.

These are the fourteen lunar days known as the **Manvantaras**. ॥ 46 ॥

### Now, he describes the Fortnightly Ancestral Rituals

Now he speaks of the **fortnightly offerings** <term>Pakṣa-śrāddha|Ancestral rites performed during a specific two-week period, usually the dark half of the month of Bhadrapada</term> beginning with the full moon <note>original: "Raka"</note> of the month of **Ashadha**. In the fifth fortnight from that full moon, starting from the full moon of the month of **Bhadrapada**, there are sixteen offerings. These are particularly sacred when the Sun is in the sign of **Virgo** <note>original: "Kanya"</note>; what is given to the ancestors then becomes inexhaustible. This sequence of sixteen offerings is considered the most excellent.

Regarding the solar transits <term>Saṅkrānti|The moment the Sun moves from one zodiac sign to another</term> and the non-intercalary months: in the twelve months beginning with **Vaishakha**, the transits of the Sun through **Aries** <note>original: "Mesha"</note> and the other signs occur in order. A month in which no solar transit occurs is called an **intercalary month** <term>Adhikamāsa|An extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar seasons</term>. Conversely, a month that contains two solar transits is a **decayed month** <term>Kṣayamāsa|A rare occurrence where a lunar month is skipped because two solar transits happen within its duration</term>. As it is heard in the tradition: "A month without a transit is an extra month; one with two transits is a lost one."

Regarding the matter of one hundred and twenty-two <note>original: "dviviṃśatyadhikaśata"</note> months, this is merely a rule. The **intercalary month** <term>Adhimāsa|An extra lunar month added to the calendar approximately every 32.5 months to keep the lunar year synchronized with the solar seasons</term> is characterized by a duration starting from the month of **Chaitra** <term>Caitra|The first month of the Hindu lunar calendar, usually falling in March-April</term> and others. Now, using the **Upajati** <term>Upajati|A classical Sanskrit poetic meter often used for instructional or philosophical verses</term> meter, he establishes the calculation for the time of the solar transit <term>Saṅkrama|The precise moment the Sun moves from one zodiac sign to the next</term>. Regarding the word "Rala," it refers to the best method for calculating the transit within the solar disc.

In the solar disc, based on the movement from the solstice <term>Ayana|The Sun's path or the period between two solstices</term>, the motion is observed. When this is added to its own eleventh part, the value in minutes <term>Kalā|A unit of angular measurement, roughly equivalent to one minute of a degree</term> and other subunits is obtained. Then, that value is multiplied by sixty—representing the sixty **ghatis** <term>Ghaṭī|A traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes; there are 60 ghatis in a full day</term>—and is further divided by the reached daily motion <term>Bhukti|The daily longitudinal motion of a planet</term> to find the exact timing.

In the "Royal Field" <note>likely a reference to a specific calculation grid or a treatise name like Rājamārtaṇḍa</note>, the calculation starting with units of **ghatis** and **palas** <term>Pala|A unit of time equal to 24 seconds, or 1/60th of a ghati</term> determines the timing of the transit. Whether in the excellent section on Aries or in other parts, this exists within the mathematical science, as it is found in the ancient texts. 55 ॥

# Commentary on the Light of Astronomy
### Chapter on Planetary Transits

<margin>

45
</margin>

Now, he explains the entry <term>Saṅkrama|The precise moment a planet moves from one zodiac sign to the next</term> of the Moon and the Sun. According to his own tradition <note>original: "svashruteh"</note>, the units of time <term>Nāḍikā|A traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes; there are 60 in a day</term> for reaching the solar transit are thirty-two <note>The text mentions "dvāviṃśan" (22) but the numerical figures provided are 32 (dvātriṃśat)</note>. These "transit-attainment" units—the smaller measures of time—are divided by the duration of the passage through one's own zodiac sign.

For the Moon and other planets, these are multiplied by the days of their own specific sign-passage <term>Bhoga|The period a planet spends in a single zodiac sign</term>, and further divided by the true daily motion <term>Spaṣṭagati|The actual observed speed of a planet, which varies throughout its orbit</term> of the Sun and other planets respectively. The result obtained from this calculation gives the duration of the transit for the Sun and the other heavenly bodies.

---

->The time units for reaching the transit are 32; divided by the passage through its own sign<-
->The inhabitants of the day <note>A poetic term for the planets</note> are divided by their own motion; by that result, the Sun's<-
->transit duration is 90. 90 ॥<-

---

This very calculation is used for practical application. In other texts, the values are given as follows: for the Moon <note>original: "vidhoh"</note>, the value is 332 <note>expressed in the 'Katapayadi' system as 'na-so-ra-ma-guna'</note>. For Mars <note>original: "bhaumasya"</note>, it is 11 minutes and 29 seconds <term>Pala|A unit of time equal to 24 seconds</term>. For Mercury <note>original: "vida"</note>, the values are 5 and 5. For Jupiter <note>original: "gurora"</note>, the value is 9 and 39. For Venus <note>original: "shukra"</note>, it is 15. For Saturn <note>original: "shaneh"</note>, the values are 5 and 8. These are the values used for the transits of the Lords of the Signs. 50.

Now, using the <note>original: "drutavilambita," a rhythmic Sanskrit poetic meter</note> meter, he explains the discernment of the transit time. If the solar transit <term>Saṅkrama|The moment the Sun enters a new zodiac sign</term> occurs before the middle of the night, the wise have declared that the merit belongs to the first half of the day, as if in a "six-fold favor" <note>original: "ṣaḍvatsala," likely referring to the six-hour window of spiritual merit</note>. However, if the transit occurs after the half-night <note>midnight</note>, then the wise say the auspicious period falls on the following day. 90.

When the Sun enters a dual-natured sign <term>Dvisvabhāva-rāśi|The zodiac signs of Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces</term>, the auspicious festival is called the "Eighty-six Faced" <note>original: "ṣaḍaśīti-mukha"</note>. ### The Auspicious Timing for Solstices and Other Transits

Now, the great sages speak of the **Auspicious Time** <term>Sukṛtakāla|The specific window of time during a solar transit deemed spiritually meritorious for rituals, bathing, and charity</term> regarding the solstices and other transits. Regarding the **Southern Solstice** <term>Dakṣiṇāyana|The sun's southward journey beginning when it enters the sign of Cancer</term>, when the Sun enters the sign of Cancer <note>original: "karka-saṃkrānti"</note>, one should understand that the sixteen **ghatikas** <note>A 'ghatika' is a traditional unit of 24 minutes; 16 ghatikas equal 6 hours and 24 minutes</note> preceding the transit are considered the meritorious time. 

Furthermore, for the transits into Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius <note>these are the four Fixed signs known as the 'Feet of Vishnu'</note>, the sixteen ghatikas are likewise known as the auspicious time. Following that, for the two transits of the **Equinoxes** <note>original: "tulājayoḥ"; referring to Libra and Aries</note>, the auspicious time is known to be in the middle—specifically, sixteen ghatikas before the Sun's entry into Aries.

->The auspicious time for the solstices and others<-
->occurring in the middle of Libra and Aries;<-
->the great sages know these times, including<-
->the Eighty-six Mouths. 90.<-

Beyond this, sixteen ghatikas are the middle time. Again, for the **Northern Solstice** <term>Uttarāyaṇa|The sun's northward journey beginning when it enters the sign of Capricorn</term>, when the entry into Capricorn <note>original: "makara saṃkrānti"</note> occurs, the auspicious time is known to be the sixteen ghatikas *following* the moment of transit. 

Finally, regarding the **Eighty-six Mouths** <term>Ṣaḍśītimukha|Auspicious solar transits occurring when the Sun enters the four mutable signs: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces</term>, when these transits into Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces occur, the sixteen ghatikas *after* the transit are known as the meritorious time. 80. <note>The number 80 here likely refers to a verse count or a sub-calculation in the commentary</note>

### The Specific Auspicious Times for the Solstices

Now, the special **Auspicious Timing** <term>Sukṛtakāla|The specific window of time during a solar transit deemed spiritually meritorious</term> for both the **Northern and Southern Solstices** <note>original: "uttara-dakṣiṇāyanayoḥ"</note> is stated. The great sages have said that these times are currently in effect as follows:

Regarding the two moments of transit <note>original: "saṃkrama-kāla"</note> for the Northern and Southern solstices, the auspicious durations are, in order, thirty <note>original: "rāma-mitāḥ"; in Sanskrit numerical code, Rama represents the number 3, often used here to denote 30</note> and thirty-five **ghatikas** <note>A unit of 24 minutes; 30 ghatikas equal 12 hours</note>. These durations were proclaimed by the sages with certainty for the benefit of the world. What is the nature of these? For the transit into a new zodiac sign, the time is again divided: thirty for the **Northern Solstice** <term>Uttarāyaṇa|The Sun's northward journey</term> and thirty-five for the **Southern Solstice** <term>Dakṣiṇāyana|The Sun's southward journey</term>.

On **Saturday** <note>original: "śanivāre"</note>, which is the day of the son of the Sun, it is **Rakshasi** <gloss>The Demonic</gloss>. 91.

Now, the author explains the specific names of the **Solar Transit** <term>Saṃkrānti|The moment the Sun enters a new zodiac sign</term> based on the constellation <term>Nakṣatra|One of the 27 lunar mansions</term> in which it occurs. <meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the classification of the Seven Transits (Ghorā, Mandā, etc.). It moves into the specific results (Phala) based on the timing of the transit during the day or night, and cites the authority of Bhatta Shankha to explain the social and worldly impacts, particularly focusing on the "Visha" and "Vaishvanara" divisions of the transit's influence.</meta>

The transit known as **Visha** <note>original: "viśoḥ", likely referring to a specific division of the transit duration</note> brings about homelessness, while the **Vaishvanara** <note>literally "belonging to all men" or "relating to the sacred fire"</note> transit makes those who experience it endowed with great happiness. However, it also creates a **Terrible Night** <note>original: "ghorātraṃ"</note>.

The **Tribhuva** <note>literally "Three Worlds"</note> transit causes people to become **eaters of the food of the lower classes** <term>Śūdrānna-bhuji|Specifically, eating food provided by the Shudra caste, traditionally viewed in these texts as a sign of social upheaval or personal degradation</term>. If the **Transit** <term>Saṃkrānti|The entry of the Sun into a zodiac sign</term> occurs during the **first watch** <term>Prahara|A traditional unit of time lasting approximately three hours</term> of the day, it results in specific outcomes for those born under it. Even if the transit is attended to for three watches, its nature is determined by the Sun’s position; if it occurs in a fierce manner, it is considered **Ugra** <note>Fierce or Terrible</note>.

Even if one possesses knowledge, the results will manifest as stated. Regarding the entry into the **Vaishya** <note>Merchant/Farmer caste</note> class, it is said that **Bhatta Shankha** <note>A historical authority on Dharmaśāstra or Jyotiṣa</note> observes that:

The transit of the Sun causes those who experience it to face various ends. If the transit occurs at the end of a watch, it yields its stated fruit. 11. If the transit occurs at the end of the **Yama** <note>A three-hour period, synonymous with Prahara</note>, it is as if the Earth is being consumed. One should remember the **Lords of the Earth** <note>original: "pṛthivīvarā", referring to Kings</note>. Half of the day is governed by the **Visha** influence. If the transit happens at sunset, it affects the **Brahmins** <note>original: "bhudevān", literally "gods of the earth"</note> and causes even the wise to eat the food of the lower classes. 73.

At
night
</margin>

The words used here are synonymous with "auspicious." In the first watch of the day, the results of the transit are described as follows: If the transit happens in the first watch, the land will be governed by a powerful ruler. Just as the Earth is girdled by the oceans, so too will it be enjoyed. Again, at midday, the transit affects the **Lords of the Earth** and kills the **Brahmins**. Again, in the afternoon, during the third part of the day, the **Vaishvanara** influence prevails until the Sun sets.

If the **Sun’s Transit** <term>Saṃkrānti|The Sun’s entry into a new zodiac sign</term> occurs at night, it destroys those such as the **Shivi** <note>An ancient tribe or community often mentioned in Vedic and Epic literature</note>, the **Jallikas** <note>Likely net-makers or hunters</note>, and the **Karikanas**. It also affects the followers of **Lallajaka** <note>original: "lallajaka", likely a reference to the school of the astronomer Lalla</note>. Furthermore, if it occurs during the transition between day and night, the light of that region—and the difference between the two—destroys the mountain-miners and those who live by the hills. At the time of the dawn's light, the transit destroys the cowherds and men of the forest. This is the ninth such indication. (74) Now, concerning the **Taitila** and other **Karanas** <term>Karaṇa|A division of time in the Hindu calendar, equal to half a lunar day (tithi)</term>, it is commanded:

The transit of the Sun during the night destroys the Shivi, the Jallikas, and the artisans. If it happens in the interval between day and night, it destroys the mountain-dwellers. If it happens at the time of dawn, the **Balava** <note>A specific Karana</note> transit destroys the cowherds. (74) If the transit of the night-maker (the Moon) or the Sun occurs during the three Karanas of **Taitila**, **Naga**, and **Tashta** <note>original: "taṣṭa", likely referring to Visti/Vishti</note>, it has a specific character. In the five Karanas known as **Bhadra**, **Vava**, **Gara**, **Kaulava**, and **Vanija**, the transit is remembered by the wise as being situated in the **Poison** <note>original: "viṣe", referring to an inauspicious timing</note> or **Nidhi** <note>literally "treasure", a specific division of the transit duration</note> sectors. (75)

The author explains the transit: If the transit occurs during the triad of Karanas—**Taitila**, **Naga**, and **Tashta**—it is a "Transit of the Three." In the same way, if the transit occurs during the five Karanas—**Bhadra**, **Vava**, **Gara**, **Kaulava**, and **Vanija**—it is recognized by the wise as a **Poison Transit** <note>original: "viṣa-saṃkramaḥ"</note>. (75)

### Concerning the Upward Transit and the Karanas

Regarding the "Upward" position: Now, when the **Sun** <note>original: "anshumato rave", literally 'the sun possessed of rays'</note> is positioned high during the three **Karanas** <term>Karaṇa|A division of time in the Hindu calendar, equal to half a lunar day</term> of **Kaulava**, **Kinstughna**, and **Garaja** <note>original: "keśaruṇa", likely a scribal error or variant for the Garaja Karana</note>, the transition occurs. 

If this transit of the Sun moves in a clockwise or southern direction, it is proclaimed by some to be auspicious. However, if the Sun's transit occurs when it is situated low <note>indicating a different celestial latitude or specific timing</note>, it becomes a causative factor for a great scarcity of grain and grass <note>original: "dhānya-tṛṇābhāva", meaning a period of drought or agricultural failure</note>. In this state, it is equal for all; it causes the destruction of the people and leads to death. (19) 

->Now, the rules for the **Muhurtas** of the **Sankranti** are stated:<-

---

When the Sun, possessed of its rays, is positioned high during the sequence of **Kaulava**, **Kinstughna**, and **Garaja**, and the transit is regulated by these signs, it is proclaimed as auspicious. (18) The specific divisions for the transit are always remembered as follows:
* Fifteen units <note>original: "pañcadaśānā", referring to 15 Muhurtas</note>
* Forty-five units (45)
* Thirty units (30)
* Eleven moments (11)

---

Always accompanied by the divine Great Sages, the transit of the Sun is known to last for fifteen **Kshanas** <note>original: "kṣaṇa", a brief measure of time</note>, which is understood to be fifteen **Muhurtas** <term>Muhūrta|A traditional Indian unit of time, roughly 48 minutes</term>. 

Again, for certain planetary alignments, the duration is forty-five (45) Muhurtas. In cases where the signs are equal, it is thirty (30) units. In other variations, it is measured as three-quarters of a Muhurta or similar fractions. These are the variations of the temporal operations as described in the **Linganushasana** <note>A reference to a systematic treatise, possibly on the gender of terms or a specific grammatical/astronomical rule-set</note>. (22)

### Now, the Discernment of Grain Prices is Declared

Regarding the phrase **"In the inferior asterisms"** <note>original: "jaghanyabhe"; referring to specific constellations considered of lower status in this astrological system</note>: when the transit occurs in these inferior asterisms, it is not prosperous for men. The **Transit of Vishnu** <note>original: "vishnu-riti"; a technical term for the Sun’s entry into a new zodiac sign</note> causes the price of grain to become **greatly expensive** <term>Mahargha|A state of dearness or high market prices for essential goods</term> until the arrival of the following month. 

Conversely, in the **even asterisms** <note>original: "sama-samjna-nakshatra"; constellations designated as 'balanced' or 'level'</note>, when the Sun's transit occurs, it produces **fair-priced grain** <note>original: "sama-sama-mulya-dhanya"; meaning stable prices accessible to the common people</note>. Furthermore:

->In an inferior asterism, the transit makes grain high-priced for one month.<-
->In a balanced asterism, the price is fair (10); in other asterisms (45), it specifically causes high prices.<-
->Duration: 18 units.<-

In the **other asterisms** <note>original: "anyabhe"; meaning those not classified as inferior or balanced</note>, it creates fair prices. Here, the phrase "the livelihood of men" refers to the availability of resources. The transit specifically causes the previously mentioned high prices, etc., in certain constellations. The term **greatly expensive** <note>original: "mahargholapakam"</note> indicates a state of high value or market scarcity in that region. (18)

### The Result of the New Moon and Solar Transit Coinciding on One Day

Now, the result is declared when the **New Moon** <term>Darsha|The precise moment of conjunction when the Moon is invisible; the final day of the lunar month</term> and the **Sun’s Transit** <term>Ravisankranti|The moment the Sun enters a new zodiac sign</term> occur on the same day of the week. 

When the **conjunction of the Sun and Moon** <note>original: "indu-ravi-samyoga"</note>—which is the definition of the New Moon day—happens on the same day that the Sun transits into a new sign, then men will face mutual destruction. Specifically, on whichever day of the week the Sun's transit occurs, if the **New Moon** <note>original: "amavasi"</note> also falls on that very day, people will perish through conflict with one another.

Furthermore, if a **Solar Eclipse** <term>Parva|A period of a lunar change or eclipse, considered a spiritually charged and often volatile time</term> also occurs on that same day, then the populace will certainly meet their end by **the edge of the sword** <note>original: "karavaladharaya"</note> and by arrows.

->When on a single day the Sun and Moon meet in conjunction, men go to their destruction.<-
->The transit leads to decay and loss...<-
->If it is an eclipse day, then death comes by arrows and the edge of the sword. (79)<-

Regarding the **Solar Transit**, the **New Moon**, and the **conjunction of the Sun and Moon**: when the Sun and Moon meet, it is called the *Darsha* day. In this context, it is explained that the conjunction of the Sun and Moon defines the New Moon. When the transit occurs on this specific day (78)...

### Prohibitions on Marriage and Rituals During Planetary Transits

Now, the author prohibits [the performance of ceremonies] such as **marriage** <note>original: "vivahadau"</note> and others on the day of a **planetary transit** <term>Graha-sankrama|The moment a planet leaves one zodiac sign and enters the next, viewed as a turbulent transition</term> and similar occasions. In that regard, the path of the **solstice** <term>Ayana|The six-month movement of the sun north or south; here referring to the transition points of the solstices</term> is highly determined. The movement of the planets, which reside in their respective celestial vehicles, involves transits. On the day of such a transit, as well as on the preceding day, [auspicious work is forbidden]. Because of the transit, both sides [of the day] are affected.

---

On the day of the transit, and particularly on the day immediately preceding it, it is considered **inauspicious** <note>original: "vimangalochite"</note>. The same applies to the days flanking the transit, which should be treated like the **time of celestial arrival** <term>nabhasrara-abhyagama-kala|The specific window when a planet is 'arriving' into a new space in the sky</term>. (80) These previously mentioned conditions are the various forms [of prohibited times]. If one considers the **sacred traditions** <note>original: "agama"</note> and the **treatises on religious duty** <term>Dharma-shastra|Ancient legal and social codes that govern Hindu life and rituals</term>, these specific periods are unsuitable for the performance of all festivals and rituals. They must always be avoided during **auspicious ceremonies** <note>original: "mangale"</note>. (9)

---

On both flanking days, and on the day of the transit itself, the same rules apply as during the time of celestial arrival; therefore, those days are not suitable for **auspicious acts** <note>original: "mangala"</note>. (80) Now, concerning the arrival of higher powers and the great avoidance: according to the **religious treatises** <note>original: "dharma-shastra"</note>, the **sacred periods** <term>Parvan|Significant points in the lunar cycle, such as the full or new moon, often requiring specific observances</term> are defined as such. What is their nature? They are the destroyers of all festival activities and all works. Again, these must always be avoided during auspicious rites. (81)

# The Determination of Auspicious and Inauspicious Combinations

Now I shall speak according to the teachings of **Narada** <note>original: "Naradine"; referring to the Narada Samhita, a classic text on astral science</note>. Day by day, clusters of **inauspicious combinations** <term>Kuyoga|A planetary alignment believed to bring obstacles or negative energy</term> may occur. Step by step, those who are **learned in the yogas** <note>original: "yogajnah"</note> must observe the specific days and the **lunar mansions** <term>Nakshatra|The 27 sectors of the sky the moon passes through, used to determine the quality of time</term> to ensure the purity and faultlessness of the timing. Just as one balances the bodily humors like **bile** <note>original: "pittavat"; likely a metaphor for the careful balancing required in medical or astrological diagnosis</note>, the cause of a successful outcome is the rising of a **desired combination** <term>Ishta-yoga|A specifically chosen planetary alignment that favors a person's goal</term>. When such a combination arises, it leads to peace and welfare. **(91)**

Now, using the **Upajati meter** <note>A classical Sanskrit poetic meter often used for instructional verses</note>, the author describes the relative strength of auspicious and inauspicious combinations. A **beneficial combination** <term>Saumya-yoga|Literally a "gentle" or "beneficial" alignment, often involving Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury</term> is not spoiled even by many faults. Conversely, a bad combination is not redeemed even by many good qualities. Wise people always perform their actions during beneficial combinations.

->Day by day, a collection of inauspicious signs may arise, even when things seem auspicious. Those who know the science of time examine every step, the day, and the lunar mansions.<-
->From the rising of the desired combination, welfare follows. **(92)** Even with many faults, a beneficial combination is not ruined.<-
->A combination is truly beneficial when spoken of by the wise through its virtues; otherwise, such actions should be avoided. **(93)** Likewise,<-
->a beneficial combination is not perceived when eclipsed by inauspicious ones. Such moments are as ruined as a divine image <note>original: "ka-deva-ri"</note> by a mockery or a smear of dung.<-
<insert>As when a high-ranking person is situated in a low place</insert> **(94)**

Travel <term>Yatra|Specifically referring to journeys for business, war, or pilgrimage which required astrological timing</term> must be undertaken only under **beneficial signs** <note>original: "saumya"</note>; other times should certainly be avoided. **(93)** <note>Note: Verse numbering in the manuscript repeats or overlaps here</note>. Furthermore, according to the opinion of some, if even a single fault falls [upon the time], it is a rejection of the best path. On the chosen day, a beneficial combination should not be viewed as spoiled [by minor faults], just as a small amount of **liquor** <note>original: "madira"</note> or a **fragment of cow dung** <note>original: "karisha-lesha"</note> might seem to pollute, yet the power of a **thousand auspicious combinations** <note>original: "sahasra yogan"</note> can overcome such small defects. **(95)**

Now, he speaks regarding the **remedy** <term>parihāra|the neutralization or avoidance of negative astrological influences</term> when there are few **virtues** <term>guṇa|auspicious qualities or strengths in an astrological chart</term> amidst many **faults** <term>doṣa|inauspicious or harmful influences</term>. The phrase "A single..." implies that one single positive quality, upon encountering and entering a vast multitude of faults, loses its own nature and perishes in an instant. It is destroyed, meaning it reaches its end. This is illustrated by the example of a **drop of water** <note>original: "malagayaviderviva"; likely a scribal variant for 'jalabindu' (water-drop)</note>: just as a pure drop of water, upon reaching a mass of intense **flames** <note>original: "jvālā-puñja"</note>, loses its own form and is consumed by the fire. For this reason, having seen the forest of faults and virtues, one must avoid the speech of the faults.

->A single virtue, when encountering a multitude of faults, is destroyed like a drop of water falling into a mass of fire.<-

->If a collection of faults is present, even a fraction of a fault must be avoided, just as a prosperous kingdom is ruined by a single vice. (85)<-

->By this logic, even if there is only a small fraction of a fault among virtues, it must be discarded. (86)<-

The word *amavāraṇa* refers to the **ocean** <note>original: "samudravācī"</note> because it is a massive body of water. Here, he explains that in a situation where there are many virtues, but a single fault resides, that fault can "burn" or reduce the virtues to ash <term>bhasmīkaroti|to incinerate or totally negate</term>. Just as a single vice can ruin a whole prosperous kingdom, a single fault residing within a collection of virtues destroys the whole. There is no doubt in this matter. For this reason, even a small portion of a fault must be **discarded** <term>vivarjanīya|that which must be avoided or given up</term> by the **wise** <note>original: "budhaiḥ"; the learned scholars or astrologers</note>. **(86)**

<summary>This page discusses the comparative strength of astrological virtues and faults, concluding that a single virtue is overwhelmed by many faults, and a single significant fault can negate many virtues, much like a drop of water in a fire or a vice in a kingdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical discussion regarding the balance between virtues and faults. While the previous page established that a single fault can destroy a multitude of virtues, this page refines that argument by forbidding the idea of "equality" or "neutrality" between the two, using both mythological examples (King Bhima) and grammatical rules (the Vedas) to explain why a predominance of virtues is the only acceptable state.</meta>

Now, he further forbids the concept of equality between **virtues** <term>guṇa|auspicious qualities</term> and **faults** <term>doṣa|inauspicious traits</term>. He says "Indeed," to indicate a common probability: a person may attain the cause of **sorrow** <note>original: "duḥkhahetu"</note> even when there is an equal balance. Why? Because when there is a **multitude** <note>original: "vrāta"</note> or a collection of virtues and non-virtues (faults), and one seeks refuge in that state of equality, it leads to ruin. To illustrate this, he provides an example of how a person meets with **calamity** <note>original: "janopadrava"</note>.

Just as when something is smeared with **collyrium** <note>original: "kajjala"|black eye-pigment or soot</note> or comes into contact with oily flowers, the state of equality (being half-clean and half-stained) is not maintained—the stain dominates. For this reason, it is said that **more virtues** <note>original: "adhikā-guṇāḥ"</note> are "better" or auspicious. In the phrase "superiority of virtues," the use of the plural or singular refers to the resulting fruit of the action.

<margin>Page/Verse 22</margin>
Regarding the refuge in an equal collection of virtues and faults: as it is said of the venerable Shiva, surely from an auspicious start one may still encounter an **obstruction** <note>original: "avāraka"</note> due to seeking a state of equality. (87) Therefore, having more virtues is superior. 

Even in the ancient story of **King Bhima** <note>A reference to the father of Damayanti in the Mahabharata</note>, his existence was marked by a multitude of virtues; however, if there is a lack of alignment in the **combination** <term>yoga|astrological or situational conjunction</term>, a difference in the "word" or outcome occurs. Again, even a single fault is not "better" just because it is active. (88) 

This is like a **grammatical discrepancy** <term>vibhakti-bheda|a mismatch in case or number</term>, such as the phrase: "The Vedas are authority." 

<note>original: "Vedāḥ pramāṇam". This is a famous linguistic example in Sanskrit where "Vedas" is plural but "Authority" is singular, used here to explain how a single principle can govern many parts.</note> (89)

Furthermore, if the divine is displeased, it does not bring delight. In the ancient time of King Bhima, **Nala** <note>The protagonist of the Nishadha kingdom</note> took hold of the path. For those like Bhima, even when seeking the auspicious, they encountered difficulties. How did the form of Nala become successful? It was not by residing in a refuge of a collection of faults. Thus, because of the lack of a proper combination, even a single fault can act like a **wheel of fire** <note>original: "vārikā-cakra"; possibly a metaphor for a revolving or inescapable cycle of harm</note> that ruins the entire action.

<summary>This page argues that an equal balance of virtues and faults is insufficient, as even a single fault can stain a person's fate, similar to how a small amount of soot stains a large area. It cites the story of King Bhima and Nala, along with grammatical rules, to prove that a predominance of virtue is required for success.</summary>

May the illustrious and radiant **Saraswati** <note>the goddess of knowledge, music, and the arts</note>, whose light is pure wisdom and who is the mistress of speech, purify all living beings with her nectar-like waters. Now, in the **fifth chapter**, having reached the topic of the results of **transits** <term>gochara|the movement of planets through the zodiac signs in relation to a person's birth sign</term> through the first house, I shall speak of their arrangement. I will explain the specific signs as the planets pass through them, or rather, I will state the results that are said to occur during these transits. I do this so that no confusion regarding the results, nor any doubt about one's fortune, shall arise among living beings. -> I speak of the results of the celestial transits, whether they arise from bad or good deeds, <-

This verse, beginning with "Yama," explains that from the heavens, in a specific order, the planets are infinite and continuous. Their positions below are as follows: they are called "Sign-Sharers" <note>original: "bhagaṇabhājaḥ"</note> because they occupy the twelve signs of the **zodiac** <term>bhagaṇa|the complete circle of the zodiac</term>. They travel according to the law of time, each following its own path. **Yama** refers to Saturn; **Guru** is Jupiter; **Kuja** is Mars; **Heli** <note>original: "Heli," a term for the Sun derived from the Greek "Helios"</note> is the Sun; **Bhargava** is Venus; **Budha** is Mercury; and the "Star-Lord" <note>original: "tārakatha"</note> is the Moon. These travel through the bodies of the signs. By this law, and through the two types of fate and time, they revolve. This was established by **Brahma** <note>the creator deity</note>. Saturn is the slowest of these...

# The Seven Types of Motion

Now, the author describes the seven-fold motion of the planets. **Equal** motion (1); **Very Swift** motion <note>original: "atinaga"; literally 'surpassing the mountains', often associated with the transition to retrograde</note> (2); **Extremely Retrograde** motion <note>original: "ativelita"; literally 'excessively wavy' or 'curved'</note> (3); **Moving** motion (4); **Fluctuating** motion (5); the motion known as **Slow** (6); and **Swift** motion (7). The "Heaven-dweller" <term>divaukas|a poetic term for a planet, literally meaning 'one who dwells in the sky'</term> possesses seven types of motion in this manner.

Now, he provides the definitions of these motions through logical explanation:

-> **Equal**, **Circular**, **Wavy**, **Fluctuating**, <-
-> and **Swift** are the motions of the Heaven-dwellers. <-
-> There is also the **Slow** motion, and through these, <-
-> the experts say there are seven paths. When the planet <-
-> moves in its diurnal circle with its **Mean Motion** <term>madhyama-gati|the average calculated speed of a planet, as opposed to its varying observed speed</term> <-
-> and matches its calculated path, it is known as **Equal** motion. 8. <-
-> When the speed is extremely low and the planet moves <-
-> **Backward** <note>original: "viloma"; meaning against the natural order of the zodiac signs</note> while stationed in a sign, <-
-> that is **Retrograde** motion. Entering the previous sign, <-
-> it becomes **Extremely Retrograde**. 9. <-

When a planet travels with its **True Motion** <term>spashta-gati|the actual, observed velocity of a planet at a specific moment</term> in such a way that it aligns with the mean calculation, then the wise call that motion of the planet **Equal** (8).

Regarding the other motions: when a planet, stationed in a particular zodiac sign, moves with **Extremely Low Speed** <note>original: "atyalpa-gati"</note> and attains a backward or "contrary" movement, that is the **Retrograde** <term>vakra|literally 'crooked' or 'curved'; the astronomical phenomenon where a planet appears to move backward in the sky</term> motion of the planet. Furthermore, when the planet, through this backward movement, leaves its current sign and enters the sign immediately preceding it, it is called **Extremely Retrograde** (9).

Now, regarding eclipses and the motions of **Retrograde** <note>original: "vakra"</note> and **Accelerated** <note>original: "atichara"</note> motion, the author prohibits the assignment of results. "Retrograde" and "Accelerated" are used here in a specific sense. 

When planets are moving in **Great Retrograde** or **Accelerated** motion, they do not bestow or surrender the "fruit" <note>the astrological result or influence</note> of the zodiac sign they are currently occupying. This is according to the teachings of ancient masters such as **Lalla** <note>an 8th-century Indian astronomer, author of the Śiṣyadhīvṛddhida Tantra</note> and **Parashara** <note>a foundational sage of Vedic astrology</note>. Their reasoning is that when the speed is unstable, the light of the planet—which is the revealer of its path—is compromised. In the morning, the light is subtle and the motion is peculiar; this is discussed in the context of the solar and lunar paths involving the deities of the directions, such as Indra, Agni, and Brahma.

In the *Samhitas* <note>encyclopedic collections of astrological lore</note>, it is stated that whether a planet travels with **Reverse Motion** <note>vakra</note> or **Excessive Motion** <note>atichara</note>, if it passes through a sign too quickly or in reverse, that Lord of the Sky <note>the planet</note> does not grant its full vision or influence to the observer. 

Even if a planet stays within the transition between two signs during its retrograde phase, its previous effects are considered canceled. This is because a person does not leave behind their own country's customs even when traveling; similarly, the planet's true nature is tied to its regular motion. 2. When a planet enters a sign with its natural, balanced motion, only then does it provide its full result. If it arrives in a distorted state, the results are inconsistent.

# Rules for the Duration of the Direct Path

# On the Helical Setting and Rising of Planets

Now, he describes the **helical setting and rising** <note>original: "astādayam"; refers to the disappearance of a planet in the Sun's light and its subsequent reappearance</note>. Regarding the "slow" planets <term>manda; the superior planets that move slower than the Sun, specifically Jupiter and Saturn</term>, and the others: when the difference in time-degrees <term>kālāmsha; a unit of arc used to measure a planet's distance from the Sun for visibility purposes</term> between the Sun and the planet is greater than the planet's own specific limit, the planet is visible. If the distance is less than its specific time-degrees, then **Jupiter** and **Saturn** enter into a state of **setting** <note>original: "asta"; becoming invisible due to proximity to the Sun</note>. 

However, there is a difference among the planets. For the **Moon**, **Mercury**, **Venus**, and **Mars**, these specific variations depend on their own time-degrees. When the distance is less than their respective time-degrees, they are considered to be set.

-> If the difference in time-degrees from the Sun is greater than these limits, <-
-> the slow planets and others remain visible. If less than their specific <-
-> degrees, they reach their helical setting. The limits are as follows: <-

-> The **Sun/Moon** <note>original: "Divākaraḥ"; usually Sun, but in this context refers to the Moon's visibility relative to the Sun</note>: 12 degrees <-
-> **Mars**: 17 degrees <note>original: "samayarā"</note> <-
-> **Mercury**: 14 degrees <note>original: "guṇojño"</note> <-
-> **Jupiter**: 11 degrees <note>original: "dṛk"</note> <-
-> **Venus**: 9 degrees <note>original: "grahā"</note> <-
-> **Saturn**: 15 degrees <note>original: "bāṇayarā"</note> <-
-> These are the time-degrees for the planets to be free from <-
-> the obscuring rays of the Sun. 15. <-

Regarding **Venus**, **Mars**, and others, the same rule applies. A **reversal** <note>original: "viparyaya"</note> of this logic is applied for the **helical rising** <note>original: "udaya"</note>. When the distance between the Sun and the planet, which was previously less than the limit, becomes greater than the specific time-degrees of that planet, then **Jupiter** and **Saturn** attain their helical rising. In the same manner, **Mercury**, **Venus**, and **Mars** proceed to their helical rising when they exceed their respective degrees. 15.

Now, having understood the sequence, he states the rule for the number of days that Mars and the other planets remain visible. "In sequence" means that these five planets, starting with Mars, having first risen in the **East** <note>original: "prācyāṃ"</note>, eventually reach their setting <term>astam; the point where a planet becomes invisible due to proximity to the Sun</term>. What is the meaning? **Mars**, having risen in the eastern direction, remains visible for **586** <gloss>650</gloss> <note>The numerical figures 586 and the written "six hundred fifty" in the vocabulary section represent different traditions of calculation; 586 is the standard synodic period for visibility in many Indian treatises</note> days before it sets. Similarly, for **Mercury**, the period is **27** days in the West.

The verse lists 551, but the commentary provides 251, which is closer to its actual visibility cycle</note>. **Saturn**, having risen in the East, reaches its setting after **339** <note>original: "ekonasaptatyadhika-śatatrayeṇa"; literally "three hundred increased by thirty-nine"</note> days. ॥ 18 ॥

Now, following this sequence, he describes the specific rule for the visibility and setting of **Venus** and **Mercury** when they are in **retrograde** <term>vakra; the apparent backward motion of a planet across the sky caused by the Earth overtaking it or vice versa</term>. The phrase "Knowers of Poetry" <note>original: "kāvyavidau"; a traditional poetic epithet for Venus and Mercury, who are associated with intellect and the arts</note> refers to Venus and Mercury. When these two are in retrograde, the duration is as follows: the number of days the planets remain visible is **two hundred and forty-eight** <note>original: "catvarimshadadhika-shatadvaye"</note>. When they have set <term>astangataḥ; the period when a planet is too close to the Sun to be seen</term> in the **East** <note>original: "pūrvasyāṃ"</note>, they remain invisible for **twenty-seven** <gloss>33</gloss> <note>The text indicates "adeva," a numerical code for 33, though the prose mentions 27; these represent variations in astronomical schools</note> days. After this, they reappear in the same direction. Then, for Venus and Mercury, after this interval, the following periods of invisibility occur: **twelve** <note>original: "dvādaśamati"</note> days and **thirty-two** <note>original: "radanāḥ"; literally "teeth," a symbolic word for the number 32</note> days respectively, after which they travel to the **West** <note>original: "pratīcyāp"</note>.

---

-> When retrograde, the visibility is 248; the setting is 33 days. <-
-> Passing through the 12 and 32 intervals, they proceed <-
-> as the "Knowers of Poetry" toward the West. 9. <-

---

<margin>Mafepa tari 9 <note>Likely an abbreviated reference to a specific commentary verse or folio: *Ma* (Maṅgala/Mars), *Fe* (Phala/Result), *Pa* (Pañcāṅga/Almanac).</note></margin>

The meaning is as follows: Starting from their rising in the **East** while in retrograde, **Venus** remains visible for a total of **two hundred and forty-eight** days. After this period, it reaches its setting point in the East once more. After **twelve** days have passed from that setting, Venus rises again in the **West**. Similarly, **Mercury** follows a comparable pattern. There is a special distinction here: while all other planets, such as **Mars**, rise in the East and set in the West, **Venus** and **Mercury** can set in the East and subsequently rise in the West <note>This refers to their transition from "Morning Star" to "Evening Star" positions relative to the Sun</note>.

Now, since the measures for the rising and setting of planets in their direct <term>avakra; the normal forward motion of a planet</term> and retrograde <term>vakra; the apparent backward motion of a planet</term> states have been determined and explained, these measures of the planets are stated only in an approximate sense <note>original: "sthūlatayā-uktaṃ"; roughly or broadly stated</note>. This is because, for the purpose of gaining true knowledge, without this specific measurement, there is no constant or steady written record <note>original: "dhruve lekhamayaṃ"; a fixed calculation or text</note> in the traditional astronomical observations <note>original: "śraute"; derived from the heard/revelatory tradition, here referring to established astronomical canon</note> regarding what is visible to the eye.

Now, he describes the characteristics of portents <term>utpāta; an unusual or abnormal natural phenomenon, often viewed as an omen</term> during this retrograde motion:

-> Because the measure of the settings and risings of direct and retrograde <-
-> planets has been stated here only roughly, it is not found in the scriptural tradition. <-
-> To understand these at all times for the range of human vision—10. When a retrograde dweller of the heavens, due to the speed of its own retrograde motion, <-
-> has a motion through the zodiac that is certainly less than its daily mean motion through the signs, then for them, it is a portentous motion... <-
-> ...according to what has been said. 11. <-

The "dweller of the heavens" <note>original: "divaukāḥ"</note> refers to a planet. When a planet, through its own retrograde motion, travels fewer degrees than the previously mentioned mean daily motion through the signs <term>rāśibhoga; the longitude a planet traverses in the zodiac</term>, then that planet's motion should certainly be known as a portent. A "dweller of the sky" is a single term for the planets. This section, because of its complexity, also discusses various types of commercial or observational divisions. 11.

Furthermore, regarding the appearance of an unobserved comet... having seen it in the presence of the Sun... for one day it is observed, therefore the "Young" and "Old" period for a comet is twenty days. 23.

Now, others state another method. The word "it is said" <note>original: "kileti"</note> implies a possibility regarding the passage of time. When a planet reaches its setting, for a duration measured by its own time-units, its state of "Oldness" <term>dārakatva; here referring to the 'Old' or weakened state of a planet, synonymous with vṛddhatva</term> persists throughout that period.
