Regarding **Sunset** <note>original: *sūryāstam*</note>: The ritual action designated for the time of sunset should be performed when that time is reached. In that context, there are other excellent rituals designated for the afternoon. 
The **Moonlight Festival** <note>original: *kaumudī-mahotsava*, here referring to the series of days around Deepavali</note> begins from the New Moon <term>darśa</term> and lasts for **five days** <note>original: *pañcadinātmakaḥ*</note>. These five days consist of the thirteenth, the fourteenth, the New Moon, the first day of the bright half, and the second day. What is the nature of this festival? It is the **Festival of Lights** <note>original: *dīpamālikā*</note>, where the success of worldly affairs and rituals is achieved through the worship of the lamps, the stars, and the day and night.
2; 5. Now, he describes **The Victory Tenth** <term>vijayādaśamī</term>. This occurs during the month of **Ashvina** <note>typically September–October</note>, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight. When the face of the night <note>early evening</note> arrives, and the stars begin to appear, that time is known by the wise as the Victory Tenth. Here, the word "Victory" refers to that which is "ever-victorious" for all people.

The ritual action designated for sunset should be performed; even a single ritual should be done in the afternoon. Here, the period starting from the New Moon lasts five days. Regarding the Moonlight Festival, I shall discuss its practical application. 5. Now, in the month of Ashvina, when the tenth day of the bright fortnight meets the onset of night, it is remembered as such. In this tradition, one should worship the **Shami tree** <note>original: *śamī*, the Prosopis cineraria, a sacred tree associated with fire and the weapons of the Pandavas</note>, which is famed as the "Fire-bearer" or associated with the **Arka** <note>the Calotropis plant or the Sun-tree</note>. This worship is for the sake of all people. When the full tenth day spans across two ends of the day <note>two consecutive sunsets</note>, then the later one is the "Victory" day. If that is not the case, the one that is free of defects is the single ruler of the ritual for worshipping the Shami tree.

Then, one should worship the Shami tree, which **destroys debts** <note>original: *ṛṇanāśinīm*</note>. What kind of Shami? One that is accompanied by the Arka tree <note>original: *arkānvitām*</note>, as is heard in the tradition. 5. Regarding the day: When the full tenth day spans both ends of the day <note>the end of the previous day and the current one</note>, then it becomes the Victory Tenth. According to the school of **Vachaspati** <note>a famous medieval legal and philosophical scholar</note>, if it is not so, it should be the time closest to the onset of night. When the Shami tree is worshipped, it becomes a means for the victory and benefit of all. 42.

# Now begins the Authority for Holika

A person seeking welfare and auspiciousness should, on the night of the **Full Moon** <term>pūrṇimā</term> in the month of **Phalguna** <note>typically February–March</note>, observe the **Hutashani** <term>hutāśanī</term> <note>literally "the consumer of oblations," referring here to the sacred bonfire of the Holi festival</note>. Whether at midnight or when the lunar mansion <term>nakṣatra</term> is appropriate, one should perform the rituals for the benefit of all. If the lighting of the fire occurs after midnight, or when the night has already passed into the next day, and the lighting happens then, or if the **Hutashani** fire is lit when the first day of the waning fortnight <term>pratipat</term> has already begun, it destroys the **Royal Prosperity** <note>original: *rājalakṣmīm*; the spiritual and material fortune of the kingdom</note>. 43. Regarding the phrase "at sunset": when the duration of the sunset is reached...

---

One seeking auspiciousness should light the **Hutashani** <note>Holi fire</note> on the night of the **Phalguna Full Moon**. If the lighting occurs during the day, or if it falls into the first day of the waning fortnight <term>pratipat</term>, it causes destruction. 43. The duration of the sunset itself is the limit, whether the **Full Moon** <term>pūrṇimā</term> is slightly more or less than that time. When this is calculated, <unclear>preḍaca</unclear> there with joined palms <note>original: *añjalinā*, a gesture of reverence</note>, the **Hutashani** should be lit at night. Then, the **Festival of Dust** <note>original: *rajamotsavaḥ*; the practice of throwing ashes or colored powder</note> shall be for the sake of **Prosperity** <note>original: *śriyai*</note>. 44. Such is the determination regarding the timing: when the Full Moon is either in excess or deficient at the time of the junction, if it is not lit properly, then the **Hutashani** is not truly "Holika." Furthermore, the celebration with the scattering of dust should bring prosperity when the night transitions into the first day of the new fortnight. 45.

->॥ 45 ॥<-

# Now, he speaks of the Vow of Parvati
<term>pārvatī-vrata</term> <note>A ritual vow dedicated to the Goddess Parvati, typically observed by women for domestic harmony and the well-being of their husbands</note>

In the month of **Ashadha** <note>The lunar month occurring around June–July</note>, starting from the **bright fortnight** <term>sita-pakṣa</term>, and specifically on the **thirteenth day** <term>trayodaśī</term> <note>original: "trayodaśī"</note>, the ritual known as **Jaya Parvati** <note>A five-day vow where women often fast and worship the Goddess with sand or clay murtis</note> is described. This vow is eternally prescribed for **women** <note>original: "yoṣitā striṇām"</note>. One should begin this vow at the correct time; it should not be started during a period of ritual impurity. <margin>j.</margin>
On the day of the twelfth, if it is properly joined [astrologically], as stated in verse 53. Regarding this vow, people should observe the **nightly vigil** <term>jāgaraṇa</term> <note>original: "rajani jāgaraṇa"</note> and other rites which bring **all-encompassing marital bliss** <term>samasta-saubhagya</term>. Having performed this, one completes the ritual. The nights are like the dark moon night <note>original: "amāvasī rajani samā"</note> in their significance.

---

<margin>Left side, page 5</margin>
<margin>The timing and method of the vow as described in the texts</margin>
On the **thirteenth day** <term>trayodaśī</term> itself, this great ritual called Jaya Parvati should be undertaken in the auspicious atmosphere of the sanctuary. One should not begin it if the timing is incorrect or during an impure state **54**. The nights of the vow, including the vigil and other practices, bestow complete **good fortune** <term>saubhagya</term>. Following that, the rituals are concluded as the night ends. Without these observances, the greatness of the woman’s [spiritual] power is not fully realized **54**. For those who desire success, the worship of **Gauri** <note>An epithet of Parvati meaning "The Fair One"</note> should be performed on the specific lunar date, for without it, the ritual is incomplete.

---

If the night is not properly occupied [by the lunar phase], the women and ladies of the household should not perform the city-wide rituals at that time. As it has been said by the masters of the ritual, the day is the husband of the rite 55. **Now he speaks of the Lunar Day of Gauri** <term>gaurī-tithi</term>. In the month of **Shravana** <note>The lunar month occurring around July–August</note>, during the **bright fortnight** <term>śukla-pakṣa</term>, the lunar date that emerges is known as Gauri’s Day. What is this day like? It is the beloved of the three worlds, dear to the gods. What kind of worship is it? It is a purification. If the sun has set at that time, then it is called the "Time of Gauri."

<margin>
Again, how should it be held? It should be performed with intense devotion and the proper ritual forms, as it is very powerful 55.
</margin>

Now, he explains the **Saptami of Shitala** <term>śītalā-saptamī</term> <note>A ritual day dedicated to Shitala, the goddess associated with cooling and protection against pox and fevers; "Saptami" refers to the seventh lunar day</note>. Regarding this, he states: This vow is to be performed by women in the month of **Nabhas** <note>The month of Shravana, occurring around July–August</note> or **Bhadrapada** <note>The month occurring around August–September</note>. It should be undertaken during the **midday period** <term>madhyāhna</term> <note>original: "madhyāhna-kāle"</note> when the seventh day is prevailing. This refers specifically to the **bright seventh** <term>śukla-saptamī</term>.

Similarly, women should observe the **Nakula Vow** <term>nākula-vrata</term> <note>A lineage-based or family observance</note> which is divided into three parts for the service of the family lineage. This is known as the **Ninth for Sons** <term>putra-navamī</term> <note>A ritual day intended to ensure the well-being and longevity of one's children</note>, which is a strong possibility for observance **56**.

Now, he speaks of the **Kajali Tritiya** <term>kajalī-tṛtīyā</term> <note>Also known as Kajari Teej, a festival where women fast and sing songs to celebrate the monsoon and pray for marital bliss</note>. In the month of **Nabhasya** <note>Another name for the month of Bhadrapada</note>, during the **dark fortnight** <term>kṛṣṇa-pakṣa</term>, when the third day rises at the time of sunrise and continues through the **midday period**, it is considered the proper time. Just as the Shitala Saptami was described in the month of Nabhasya for women, this **Ninth day** in the bright fortnight should be observed by those following the threefold Nakula vow **59**. In the month of Nabhas, during the bright fortnight at sunrise, the timing is...

<margin>It should be performed for the fulfillment of all desires, according to the response of the sage Vashishtha 58 ||</margin>

...one should accept the third day known as **Kajala** <note>original: "kajalā"</note>. On this third day, if it is joined with the month of Nabhas, it is said to be "pregnant" <note>original: "garbhāsta"</note> with significance until it reaches the concluding rites **59**. In the month of Bhadrapada, on the bright twelfth day, there is the observance known as **Abhaya** <note>original: "abhaya-saṃjñikā"</note>. This should be performed by women following the proper sequence of time for the **attainment of their desires** <term>kāma-siddhaye</term> **58**.

When the day rises again, that third day should once more be considered the Kajali day. Because she is the wife of the creator-lord Prajapati, it is highly meritorious. The third day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada is particularly distinguished; if it is not found then, it is sought in the latter part. This results in a sevenfold multiplication of merit **57**. He now speaks of the **Auspicious Abhaya Dvadashi** <term>śubhābhaya-dvādaśī</term> <note>The "Auspicious Twelfth of Fearlessness," a day dedicated to the worship of Vishnu to remove all fears</note>. In the month of Bhadrapada, women should observe the twelfth day known as **Abhaya**, occurring during the bright fortnight, following the prescribed seasonal timing.

Now, he explains the **Vow of the Infinite** <term>ananta-vrata</term> <note>A significant ritual dedicated to Lord Vishnu in his form as Ananta (the Infinite), usually involving the tying of a sacred thread with fourteen knots</note>. He says: regarding the **midday period** <term>madhyāhna</term> in the month of **Bhadrapada** <note>August–September</note>, during the **bright fortnight** <term>sitā</term> <note>original: "sitā"; referring to the waxing moon</note>, the Infinite Vow should be observed when the **fourteenth lunar day** <term>caturdaśī</term> prevails at midday. This is the conclusion of the wise regarding the proper time for the ritual. When this fourteenth day is united with the vow, it provides freedom from the fear of fruitlessness for the practitioner **55**.

Now, he explains the **Vow of the Sun** <term>arka-vrata</term> <note>original: "arkavrata"; Arka is a name for the Sun God, Surya</note>. The wise man says: following the authority of **Hemadri** <note>A 13th-century scholar and prime minister whose encyclopedic work, the "Chaturvarga Chintamani," is the definitive guide for ritual timings in medieval India</note>, one should perform the Sun’s vow on a **Sunday** <term>ravi-dine</term>. One should perform it during a **solar transit** <term>saṅkrame</term> <note>The moment the sun moves from one zodiac sign to another</note>, specifically during the **first watch of the day** <term>prathama-prahara</term>. This includes rituals such as worship, making offerings, and specific rules for eating.

The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhadrapada, occurring at midday, is celebrated as the **Vow of the Infinite** for women. This has been handed down by the wise as a constant practice to remove the fear of failure for those born under certain stars **72**. Regarding the **Vow of the Sun**, on a Sunday, and always during the first watch of the day—or during the transit of another day—one should perform worship, giving of gifts, and the ritual meal. These acts ensure the fulfillment of **progeny, merit, health, and wealth**. Likewise, in all solar-related vows, when the transit occurs on his [the practitioner's] own day, the acts of bathing, giving, worship, and eating are performed to please the planets and achieve one's desired goals **6**.

Likewise, if a solar transit always occurs on its own day, or in all the various solar vows or during the vows of the planets, it becomes beneficial for that man. The planets grant his heart's desires when he performs the rituals of bathing, giving, worship, and eating.

# <gloss>Auspiciousness</gloss> Now he describes the meritorious results of the eclipses of the Sun and others. Regarding the phrase **"On the Sun's day"** <note>original: "ravau rave"; referring to a solar eclipse occurring on a Sunday</note>: when a solar eclipse occurs on a Sunday <term>ravi-vāra</term>, or during a **Solar Transit** <term>ravi-saṅkrame</term> <note>the moment the sun enters a new zodiac sign</note>, it is of great significance.

If an eclipse of the Sun <term>sūrya-uparāga</term> occurs, or if an eclipse of the Moon <term>candra-uparāga</term> occurs on a **Monday** <note>original: "rāja-dine"; literally "the King's day," a poetic term for Monday, the day of the Moon</note> or during a transit, the merit <term>puṇya</term> earned is equal to the measure of the eclipse itself. If the eclipse occurs on these specific days and during a transit, the merit for rituals such as **chanting** <term>japa</term> is multiplied many times over **11**. Regarding the **contact** <term>sparśe</term> <note>the beginning phase of an eclipse</note>: at the time of contact, one should observe the eclipse, and then perform the ritual bath <term>snāna</term> and chanting. This is the established rule. In the middle of the moon's eclipse...

---

7, Transit 8.
</margin>

</margin>
When an eclipse occurs on a Sunday or a Monday, combined with a transit, the merit is as previously described. By these two factors, the fruit of chanting and other rituals is doubled **12**. After the contact has occurred, one should perform the bath, chanting, and other rites. One should perform **offerings in the sacred fire** <term>havana</term> at the beginning and in the middle of the eclipse. When the eclipse is **releasing** <term>vimucyamāne</term> <note>the ending phase</note>, one should give **charity** <term>dāna</term> according to their own capacity. After the release is complete, one must perform a ritual bath **13**.

Now, regarding the **viewing of an eclipse by a pregnant woman** <term>garbhavatī</term>: she should never view the eclipse. If she sees both eclipses—the lunar and the solar—there is a danger of **injury** <term>hiṃsā</term> or **deformity** <term>vaikalya</term> to the child in her womb. Her offspring may suffer from wasting or weakness. For as long as the Moon and the Sun are being seized by the eclipse <note>original: "rāhu-vilokane"; referring to the shadow-demon Rahu swallowing the celestial bodies</note>, for that long, she must remain cautious so that no harm comes to the child **65**.

<margin>
...at that time, the child is like one dead, or suffers greatly; there should be no exhaustion.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions regarding eclipses from page 354. While the previous page established the merit of performing rituals during solar and lunar eclipses, this page provides specific dietary restrictions and rules for ritual purification (snāna) depending on when the eclipse occurs and when the celestial body sets.</meta>

Regarding the phrase **"setting while eclipsed"** <note>original: "grastāstam"; refers to the Sun or Moon setting before the eclipse has finished</note>: when the Sun or Moon <term>ravīndu</term> sets while still under the influence of an eclipse, a wise person should not eat. 3

One should eat again only after the celestial body has been seen as clear. For the Moon <term>vidhoḥ</term> <gloss>3</gloss>, one should avoid eating for **two quarters** <term>prahara-dvayam</term> <note>a prahara is approximately 3 hours, so about 6 hours</note>. For the Sun <term>raveḥ</term>, one should avoid eating for **four watches** <term>yāma-catuṣṭayam</term> <note>approximately 12 hours</note>. This is the general rule for a lunar eclipse **25**. 

Now, he explains the purification of the **lunar day** <term>tithi</term> at the time of the eclipse: as long as the Sun <term>bhānumān</term> does not rise <gloss>not</gloss>, until then...

---

When the Sun or Moon goes to its setting while eclipsed, one should not eat. One should eat again only when the body is seen to be clear. Avoid eating for the first two quarters of the Moon's eclipse and four watches for the Sun **25**. If an eclipse occurs, one should not perform the ritual bath <term>snāne</term> for birth-impurity, illness, or menstruation until the Sun rises; one must not eat before then. For the purpose of this ritual, the **prevailing lunar day** <term>tātkālikī tithi</term> is the one used for the procedure. 
->**determined for the Moon 26** ॥<-

---

Regarding the ritual bath for birth, illness, or menstruation during an eclipse: one should not assume purification <term>śuddhi</term> or perform the bath for these conditions during the eclipse itself. Rather, if it occurs at night, the "contemporary" or "prevailing" lunar date—the one actually occurring at that specific time—is the one recognized by the wise for the performance of **ancestral rites** <term>śrāddha</term>. This completes the rule **26** ॥

It also clarifies which lunar day (tithi) should be used for ancestral offerings when an eclipse complicates the calendar.</summary>

Now he describes the definitions of the units of time beginning with the **Moment** <note>original: "kshana"; here referring to a specific astronomical window before sunrise</note>. When four **ghatis** <term>ghati</term> <note>a ghati is a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes; four ghatis is approximately 96 minutes</note> remain at the end of the night, that time is known as the **Moment** <term>kshana</term>. Following that period, when one additional part is added, that time is declared to be **Dawn** <term>arunodaya</term> <note>literally "the rising of Aruna," the charioteer of the Sun</note>. Likewise, when another part is added to the Dawn, it is remembered as the time of **Early Morning** <term>ushas</term>. At the end of the night, when the day is just slightly beginning and two **ghatis** <term>ghati</term> <note>about 48 minutes</note> remain, that is specifically remembered as **Sunrise** <term>suryodaya</term>.

> When four ghatis remain [before sunrise], it is the **Moment** <term>kshana</term>. From that time, with one part added, it is **Dawn** <term>arunodaya</term>. 
> With one more part added, it is the time of **Early Morning** <term>ushas</term>; when two ghatis remain, it is called **Sunrise** <term>suryodaya</term>. ॥ 10 ॥ 
> The wise should apply this timing to sacrifices and other rituals for the gods. 
> For the time of the ancestors, one should always exclude the three-fifth parts. 18 ॥

**Regarding Ritual Action** 9. Now he explains the **rule for the timing of ancestral rites** <term>shraddha-kala-niyama</term>. Regarding what was said about "sacrifices and so on": for all rituals concerning the gods and the ancestors, this should be understood by the **wise** <term>manishibhih</term> <gloss>learned scholars</gloss>. What is to be understood? That one should set aside the five-part division of time and exclude the three-fifth part. 18 ॥ ॥ ॥

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the proper timing for rituals. Now, it was stated that the **three-fifth part** <note>original: "tripecabhaga"; a specific division of the day</note> of time is not desired for **Ancestral Rites** <term>shraddha</term>. Here, the author explains the rule regarding the **Dedication of the Blue Bull** <term>nilodvaha</term> <note>a ritual where a bull is consecrated and set free, often performed for the benefit of deceased ancestors</note> and other rites.

Regarding the *Nīlodvāha*: it is like an ancestral rite performed for cattle. When the beneficial time has arrived, the **Cattle Marriage** <term>go-vivaha</term> <note>a synonym for the bull dedication ceremony</note> should occur according to the sequence to be described.

"Nayā" <note>original: "नयेति"</note> is used here as a qualifier for the action. What does this mean? On the day the *Nīlodvāha* and related rituals are performed, it is not strictly mandatory <note>original: "avashyam kartavyam"</note> to fix a specific **astrological rising sign** <term>lagna</term>. The details regarding the *Nīlodvāha* and subsequent rites will be clarified <gloss>known</gloss> from this.

->The **Dedication of the Blue Bull** <term>nilodvaha</term> is like an ancestral rite; when the beneficial time arrives, let the **Cattle Marriage** <term>go-vivaha</term> take place according to the sequence of stages.<-
->55. The **Daily Ancestral Rite** <term>nitya-shraddha</term> is constant, while the **Bull Dedication** <term>nilodvaha</term> is occasional. If performed according to the rules, it should proceed in its prior state, and not otherwise...<-
->7.<-

It happens in this way; there is no specific time-regulator for that. 25. "Daily" <note>original: "nityam"</note> means certain. In the **Daily Ancestral Rite**, the *Nīlodvāha* and the cattle-rite are mutually occasional. What does this mean? It was previously stated that *Śrāddha* should be performed during a time that excludes the **three-fifth part**. However, for the Daily Rite and the *Nīlodvāha* ceremony, that restrictive rule does not apply. In the prior state where the *Nīlodvāha* work proceeds, at the time of the ritual, that "three-fifth part" is not excluded. 7.

Now, the author speaks briefly regarding the **Dedication of the Blue Bull** <term>nilodvaha</term> <note>a ritual where a bull is consecrated and set free to ensure the salvation of ancestors</note>, beginning with the word *Nāsatya*. *Nāsatya* refers to the **Twin Physicians** <term>ashvins</term> <note>deities of the Ashvini constellation</note>. *Anala* refers to the **Fire God** <note>deity of the Krittika constellation</note>. The "Constellation of Vishvakarma" <note>the divine architect</note> refers to the constellation **Chitrakila** <term>chitra</term> and its presiding deity. *Vishakha* and the others refer to the names of the constellations. The months associated with these are **Ashvina**, **Kartika**, **Chaitra**, and **Vaishakha**. Among these seven months, the **Ancestral Rite** <term>pitru-karya</term> <note>specifically the Shraddha ritual</note> is performed. Now, he prohibits the **Dedication of the Blue Bull** during certain astrological alignments, such as when the **Sun is in Leo** <term>simha</term>. Specifically, when Jupiter or Venus are "set" <note>original: "astagau"; meaning heliacally set or combust, rendered invisible by the sun's glare</note>, and similarly during the intercalary months.

->The constellations of the Ashvins, Agni, Vishvakarma, and the deity of Vishakha; the months derived from these are for the ancestors. Thus, those who seek the union with the virtuous should perform the ceremony according to the rules of the **Bull Sacrifice** <term>vrsotsarga</term>. 71. Not when the Sun is in Leo, nor when Jupiter or Venus are set, nor in the intercalary month or the intercalary year—the wise know these are not for the **Blue Bull Dedication** ritual. Nor should it be done at the holy sites of **Gaya** or the **Godavari** without first performing the **Daily Ancestral Rite** <term>ahnika</term>. 72.<-

The "union with the virtuous" refers to the breath of life or those worthy of **Dharma** <note>universal law/righteousness</note>. Why are they considered such? Because of the rules governing the **Bull Sacrifice** <term>vrsotsarga-vidhana</term>. Regarding the Blue Bull Dedication and other such rites: when **Venus** <term>shukra</term> or **Jupiter** <term>sita</term> have set <gloss>are combust</gloss>, or during the three types of intercalary months or years, the wise know the rules of the **Blue Bull Dedication** <note>meaning they know to avoid these times</note>. They do not perform them. This means that at holy sites like **Gaya** or the **Godavari** river, one must not perform these rites without first completing the **Initial Daily Rite** <term>prathama-ahnika</term>, which is the first **Ancestral Offering** <term>shraddha</term>. One should avoid these [prohibited times and conditions]. 72.

It emphasizes that at holy sites like Gaya, the daily ancestral rites must take precedence before this specific bull sacrifice can occur.</summary>

Now, the author speaks briefly regarding the **Dedication of the Blue Bull** <term>nilodvaha</term> <note>a complex Vedic ritual where a bull is consecrated and released to wander freely, believed to provide eternal satisfaction to one's ancestors</note>, beginning with the word *Nāsatya*. *Nāsatya* refers to the **Twin Physicians** <term>ashvins</term> <note>the celestial twin deities who preside over the constellation Ashvini</note>. *Anala* refers to the **Fire God** <note>the deity presiding over the constellation Krittika</note>. The "Constellation of Vishvakarma" <note>the divine architect of the gods</note> refers to the constellation **Chitra** <term>chitra</term> and its presiding deity. *Vishakha* and the others refer to the names of the constellations. The months associated with these are **Ashvina** <note>September–October</note>, **Kartika** <note>October–November</note>, **Chaitra** <note>March–April</note>, and **Vaishakha** <note>April–May</note>. Among these seven months, the **Ancestral Rite** <term>pitru-karya</term> <note>specifically the Shraddha ritual performed for the deceased</note> is performed. Now, he prohibits the **Dedication of the Blue Bull** during certain astrological alignments, such as when the **Sun is in Leo** <term>simha</term>. Specifically, the ceremony should not occur when Jupiter or Venus are "set" <note>original: "astagau"; this refers to heliacal setting, where a planet becomes invisible because it is too close to the Sun</note>, and similarly, it is forbidden during intercalary months <note>an extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it aligned with the solar seasons</note>.

->The constellations of the Twin Physicians, the Fire God, the Divine Architect, and the deity of Vishakha; the months derived from these are the proper times for the ancestors. Thus, those who seek to join the company of the virtuous should perform the ceremony according to the rules of the **Bull Sacrifice** <term>vrsotsarga</term>. 71. Not when the Sun is in the sign of Leo...<-

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->Jammu<-

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. In the library’s categorization system, 'Gha' is the fourth letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, likely indicating a specific section or shelf.</note>
**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). This is a celebrated treatise focused on the selection of auspicious moments for various life events and astronomical calculations.</note>
**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. Although the text bears the name of India's most famous poet, scholars generally believe it was composed by a later author of the same name who specialized in the astral sciences.</note>
**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This number indicates the total count of folios (individual leaves) contained within this manuscript bundle.</note> **Age** .............
**Subject** Astrology and Astronomy <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (Jyotiṣam). This traditional field of study encompasses both the mathematical calculation of planetary positions and their interpreted influence on human affairs.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
## Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. The character 'Gha' is the fourth consonant of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a classification or shelf-list marker.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). This is a celebrated treatise on electional astrology, providing guidance on the most auspicious times for performing various life rites and religious ceremonies.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. While the text is traditionally attributed to the famous 4th-5th century poet Kalidasa, modern scholars believe it was composed by a later author of the same name, or attributed to the legend to lend the work prestige.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This number indicates the total count of folios—individual leaves—comprising the manuscript.</note> **Age** .............

**Subject** <term>Astrology and Astronomy</term> <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (*Jyotiṣam*). This traditional "science of light" involves the study of celestial bodies to track time and predict the influence of the stars on human affairs.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
## Jammu

**No.** 846 - D <note>original: "८४६ - घ" (846-gha); the letter 'Gha' is the fourth letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a sub-index for library filing.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astronomer</term> <note>original: "Jyotirvidābharaṇam" (ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्). This is a classical Sanskrit treatise focusing on *Muhurta* (the selection of auspicious moments) and various aspects of mathematical astronomy.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: "Kālidāsa" (कालिदास). Although the text is attributed to Kalidasa, the name of India's most celebrated poet and dramatist, scholars generally consider this specific technical work to be the product of a later author using the same name or writing within that prestigious tradition.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: "३५६"; this number refers to the total count of individual manuscript folios, or pages, contained within the bundle.</note> **Age** ........................

**Subject** <term>Astral Sciences</term> <note>original: "Jyotiṣam" (ज्योतिषम्). In the Indian tradition, this term refers to the integrated study of astronomy, mathematics, and astrology.</note>

# Shri Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library, Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gh <note>original: "८४६- घ"; the letter 'Gh' (Gha) is the fourth consonant of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a shelf-mark or sub-classification index.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: "Jyotirvidābharaṇam" (ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्). This is a significant Sanskrit treatise on <term>muhūrta</term> (electional astrology)—the ancient practice of selecting the most spiritually and cosmically auspicious moments for rituals, travels, and life events.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: "कालिदास". Although the text is traditionally attributed to the most famous poet of classical India, scholars generally consider this specific astrological work to be the product of a later writer using the prestigious name as a pseudonym.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: "३५६". This indicates the total number of individual folios (handwritten leaves) contained in this specific manuscript volume.</note> **Age** __________

**Subject** <term>Astrology and Astronomy</term> <note>original: "Jyotiṣam" (ज्योतिषम्). This refers to the traditional Indian "science of light," which encompasses mathematical astronomy, timekeeping, and the interpretation of celestial movements.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->Jammu<-

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: "८४६-घ"; the number is written in Devanagari digits. The letter "Gha" likely refers to a specific shelf or category classification within the library's system.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: "Jyotirvidābharaṇam" (ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्). This is a significant Sanskrit treatise on electional astrology, used to determine the most auspicious times for various life events and religious ceremonies.</note>

**Author** <term>Kalidasa</term> <note>original: "कालिदास". Although this work is attributed to the world-renowned poet Kalidasa, most modern scholars believe it was written by a later author who adopted the name to give the text greater prestige and authority.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: "३५६"; this represents the total number of leaves or folios contained within this specific manuscript.</note> **Age** ........................

**Subject** <term>Astral Sciences</term> <note>original: "Jyotiṣam" (ज्योतिषम्). This is the traditional Indian field of study that combines what we now call astronomy and astrology, used for timekeeping and divination.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->**Jammu**<-

**No.** 846-Gha <note>original: "८४६-घ"; the number 846 is followed by the Sanskrit letter 'Gha,' which acts as a serial or category marker in the library's filing system.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Star-Knower</term> <note>original: "Jyotirvidābharaṇam" (ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्). This is a classical Sanskrit treatise on the "astral sciences" (Jyotiṣa), which in ancient India encompassed astronomy, mathematics, and astrology. The title implies the text is a decorative or essential jewel for the scholar of the heavens.</note>

**Author** <term>Kalidasa</term> <note>original: "कालिदास". While the manuscript bears the name of India's most famous classical poet (author of "The Cloud Messenger"), historians believe this specific technical text was written by a later scholar who adopted the prestigious name as a pseudonym.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: "३५६"; this indicates the manuscript contains 356 individual folios or pages.</note> ..................... **Age** .....................

**Subject** <term>Astral Science</term> <note>original: "Jyotiṣam" (ज्योतिषम्). This field of study was one of the six "limbs" of Vedic knowledge, essential for calculating the timing of rituals and understanding the movement of celestial bodies.</note>

## Jammu

**No.** 846-D <note>original: "८४६- घ"; the manuscript number is written in Devanagari numerals. The letter "Gha" (घ) is the fourth letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, serving as a category marker similar to the letter "D" in Western systems.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astronomer</term> <note>original: *Jyotirvidābharaṇam*. The title suggests a "jewel" or "decoration" of knowledge intended for those who study the movements of the stars and planets.</note>

Although the label attributes this work to the legendary classical poet Kalidasa, scholars typically categorize this as a "pseudo-Kalidasa" text, likely written by a later astronomer and attributed to the great poet to grant the work greater authority.</note>

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: "८४६- घ"; the character "Gha" is the fourth letter of the Devanagari alphabet, used here to denote a specific shelf or subject category within the library’s archival system.</note>

**Title** *The Ornament of the Astrologer* <note>original: "ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्" (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). This is a classical Sanskrit treatise focusing on <term>Muhūrta</term>—the science of determining auspicious moments for religious rituals, travel, and business.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: "कालिदास"; though traditionally attributed to the famous 5th-century poet Kalidasa (author of *Shakuntala*), this specific astrological work is widely considered by historians to be the product of a later author who used the name as a pseudonym to lend the text classical authority.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: "३५६"; this indicates the manuscript consists of 356 folios (loose-leaf pages).</note> ........................ **Age** ........................

**Subject** Astrology <note>original: "ज्योतिषम्" (Jyotiṣam); one of the six auxiliary disciplines of the Vedas, encompassing both mathematical astronomy and predictive astrology.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
## Jammu

<meta>The library, located in Jammu, India, holds one of the most significant collections of Sanskrit manuscripts in the world, largely assembled under the patronage of the Dogra kings in the 19th century.</meta>

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: "८४६ - घ"; the Devanagari numeral and the letter 'Gha' serve as a shelf-mark or classification code to locate the item within the library's specific storage cabinets.</note>

**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: "ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्" (<term>Jyotirvidābharaṇam</term>); a major Sanskrit work on <term>muhūrta</term> (auspicious timing) used to determine the most favorable moments for rituals, marriages, and other life events.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: "कालिदास"; while the text is attributed to the famous 4th-century poet Kalidasa, modern scholars categorize this as a "pseudo-Kalidasa" work, likely composed in the late medieval period (roughly 13th–16th century) by a different scholar using the illustrious name.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: "३५६"; this indicates the number of individual leaves or folios that make up the manuscript, suggesting a very substantial and detailed copy.</note> **Age** ........................

**Subject** Astral Sciences <note>original: "ज्योतिषम्" (<term>Jyotiṣam</term>); a traditional Indian science that encompasses both mathematical astronomy (the movement of stars and planets) and astrology (the influence of those movements on human affairs).</note>

# Shri Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library, Jammu

**No.** <insert>846 - Gh</insert> <note>original: ८४६ - घ. The character 'Gh' likely indicates a specific shelf-mark or thematic category within the library’s extensive catalog.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library, Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ; 'Gha' is the fourth consonant of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a shelf-mark or classification code within the library's filing system.</note>

**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: <term>Jyotirvidābharaṇam</term> (ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्); a classic Sanskrit treatise focused on <term>Muhūrta</term>—the science of selecting the most auspicious times for rituals, ceremonies, and daily actions.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास; while the text claims to be by the legendary poet Kalidasa (the author of *Shakuntala*), scholars typically attribute this astrological work to a later author from approximately the 12th to 16th century who adopted the famous name.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६; this indicates the manuscript contains 356 individual leaves or folios, making it a substantial volume.</note>  **Age** ...........

**Subject** Astrology and Astronomy <note>original: <term>Jyotiṣam</term> (ज्योतिषम्); one of the six auxiliary disciplines of the Vedas, which includes the study of celestial bodies, timekeeping, and divination.</note>

# Shri Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library, Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ; the letter "Gha" is the fourth consonant of the Sanskrit alphabet, here functioning as a classification or shelf-mark indicator.</note>

**Title** **The Ornament of the Astrologer** <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). In the Sanskrit tradition, the word "ornament" (<gloss>ābharaṇam</gloss>) is frequently used in titles to suggest that the text "adorns" or enhances the intellect of the practitioner. The term <term>Jyotirvid</term> literally means "one who knows the lights," referring to an expert in the stars and planets.</note>

**Author** **Kalidasa** <note>original: कालिदास; this name is shared with India's most famous classical poet (c. 4th-5th century CE). However, this specific work on astronomy is widely considered by historians to be the product of a later author who adopted the prestigious name to provide the text with immediate authority.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६; this number refers to the total count of individual manuscript leaves, or folios, making up this specific copy.</note> <space> **Age** ____________

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
### Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. The letter 'Gha' is the fourth letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, functioning here as a shelf-mark or classification code.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). This is a classical Sanskrit treatise on "Muhurta" or electional astrology—the practice of calculating the most spiritually and cosmically auspicious moments for rituals, travel, and life transitions.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. Though attributed to the legendary 4th-century poet Kalidasa, historians generally consider this specific astrological work to be the product of a later scholar who adopted the famous name to lend the text greater authority.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This refers to the total number of hand-written leaves, or folios, that comprise this manuscript.</note> **Age** ..........................

**Subject** <term>Astronomy and Astrology</term> <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (*Jyotiṣam*). Known as the "Science of Light," this traditional discipline includes both the mathematical calculation of planetary positions and the study of their influence on human affairs.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
### Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. The character 'Gha' is a Sanskrit numeral/alphabetical marker used for classification.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). This is a well-known treatise on electional astrology (Muhurta), used to determine the most auspicious times for performing various life rituals and ceremonies.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->## Jammu<-

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. The character 'Gha' is the fourth consonant of the Devanagari alphabet, used here as a shelf-mark or classification indicator.</note>

**Title** *The Ornament of the Astrologer* <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). This is a significant Sanskrit treatise on electional astrology, or "Muhurta," used to calculate the most auspicious times for ceremonies and daily activities.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. While the text is traditionally attributed to the famous classical poet Kalidasa, modern scholars generally consider this work to be by a later medieval author writing under the same prestigious name.</note>

### Shri Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->Jammu<-

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. This is the archival shelf-mark; "Gha" is the fourth letter of the Devanagari alphabet, likely used for categorization or series identification.</note>

**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). A classic treatise focused on <term>Muhurta</term>—the selection of auspicious moments—and various mathematical calculations used in astrology.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. While the text bears the name of India’s most famous poet (c. 4th–5th century CE), scholars generally agree that this specific astronomical work was composed by a later author adopting the name as a tribute or to lend the work authority.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This indicates the total number of folios, or individual hand-written sheets, that make up the manuscript.</note> **Age**

**Subject** Astronomy and Astrology <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (*Jyotiṣam*). In the Sanskrit tradition, this "Science of Light" includes mathematical astronomy, the calculation of calendars, and the interpretation of celestial influences.</note>

<note>original: कालिदास. Although the text claims to be the work of the legendary Sanskrit poet Kalidasa (author of *Shakuntala*), most historians believe this technical work was written by a later scholar using the famous poet’s name to imbue the text with prestige and authority.</note>

<note>original: ज्योतिषम् (*Jyotiṣam*). In the Indian tradition, this term encompasses the <term>Vedanga</term> (an auxiliary science of the Vedas) that includes mathematical astronomy, the calculation of calendars, and the interpretation of celestial omens.</note>

**Title** <insert>The Ornament of the Astrologer</insert> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). A poetic title for a technical manual, suggesting that the knowledge within serves as a 'jewel' or 'decoration' for a practitioner of the astral sciences.</note>

**Author** <insert>Kalidasa</insert> <note>original: कालिदास. While the text claims the authorship of the famous 5th-century poet Kalidasa, historians generally view this as a later work of technical astrology attributed to his prestigious name.</note>

### Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
#### Jammu

**No.** 846 - Gha <note>original: ८४६ - घ. The number is written in Devanagari numerals; 'Gha' is the fourth letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a shelf-mark or classification category.</note>

**Title** **<term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term>** <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). The title suggests a work intended to serve as a decorative or essential "jewel" of knowledge for practitioners of the astral sciences.</note>

**Author** **Kalidasa** <note>original: कालिदास. While this shares the name of the most famous classical Sanskrit poet, scholars generally believe this specific astrological work was composed by a later author using the name as a pseudonym to grant the text greater prestige.</note>

**Extent** **356** <note>original: ३५६. This indicates the total number of leaves or folios, making this a very substantial manuscript.</note> **Age** ........................

**Subject** **<term>Astronomy and Astrology</term>** <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (*Jyotiṣam*). This traditional science encompasses both the mathematical mapping of stars (astronomy) and the interpretation of their influences (astrology).</note>

**Title** <insert>The Ornament of the Astrologer</insert> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). This title describes a text that serves as a "decoration" or essential guide for practitioners of the celestial sciences. **Title** **The Ornament of the Astrologer** <note>original: <term>Jyotirvidābharaṇam</term>. This is a classical treatise on <term>Jyotish</term> (astral sciences), specifically focusing on electional astrology—the art of choosing the most auspicious times for various life events and religious ceremonies.</note>

**Author** **Kalidasa** <note>original: कालिदास. While the text claims to be the work of the famous 4th-century poet Kalidasa, internal evidence and linguistic style lead modern historians to believe it was composed much later, likely around the 16th century.</note>

**Subject** **Astral Sciences** <note>original: <term>Jyotish</term> (ज्योतिषम्). This traditional Sanskrit term encompasses both mathematical astronomy and the interpretive science of astrology.</note>

**No.** 846-Gh <note>original: ८४६- घ. The number 846 is written in Sanskrit numerals. The letter 'Gh' (the fourth consonant of the Devanagari alphabet) likely indicates a specific shelf or category within the library's classification system.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: *Jyotirvidābharaṇam* (ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम्). A major Sanskrit treatise focused on astrology and the determination of auspicious times (*muhūrta*). The title metaphorically suggests that this knowledge is a "decoration" or "jewel" for a learned practitioner.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. While this work is traditionally attributed to Kalidasa—India’s most legendary poet—modern historians generally believe this specific astrological text was written by a later scholar who adopted the famous name to lend authority to the work.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This indicates the manuscript consists of 356 folios (leaves), marking it as a particularly long and comprehensive copy.</note> **Age** __________

**Subject** <term>Astrology and Astronomy</term> <note>original: *Jyotiṣam* (ज्योतिषम्). This is the traditional Indian science of celestial observation, which encompasses both the mathematical calculation of planetary movements and their interpreted influence on earthly events.</note>

1 || Salutation to the Illustrious Ganesha || <note>original: *Śrī Gaṇeśāya Namaḥ*. A standard opening formula in Hindu manuscripts, invoking the elephant-headed deity of wisdom and the remover of obstacles to ensure the successful completion of the work.</note>

May that elephant-faced form <note>Ganesha</note> be pleased with you—the one by whose grace the primordial Lord, the wielder of the Pinaka bow <note>original: *Pinākī*, an epithet for Lord Shiva</note>, becomes filled with a flood of supreme bliss during the twilight hours and clearly performs his dance throughout the three worlds. || 1 || <note>This verse creates a poetic link between Ganesha and his father Shiva, whose cosmic dance (Tandava) sustains the universe.</note>

I am composing this work titled <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> to the best of my ability; it is the finest essence and the crowning decoration for the entire collection of sacred scriptures. || 2 || <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (*Jyotirvidābharaṇam*). The author suggests that astrology is the most vital "ornament" or accessory to the Vedas and other traditional sciences.</note>

This work, which always embodies the essence of all the sciences, was composed by Kalidasa to be pure, pleasing to the mind, and a source of delight for the learned. || 3 || <note>original: कालिदास (*Kālidāsa*). The text attributes itself to the most famous poet of classical Sanskrit literature. However, historians generally categorize this specific astronomical treatise as a later "pseudo-Kalidasa" work, likely from the 16th century, using the famous name to lend the text prestige.</note>

May that elephant-faced form <note>Ganesha</note> be pleased with you—the one by whose grace the primordial Lord, the wielder of the Pinaka bow <note>original: *Pinākī*, an epithet for Lord Shiva</note>, becomes filled with a flood of supreme bliss during the twilight hours and clearly performs his dance throughout the three worlds. || 1 || <note>This verse creates a poetic link between Ganesha and his father Shiva, whose cosmic dance (Tandava) sustains the universe.</note>

I am composing this work titled <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: *Jyotirvidābharaṇam*</note> to the best of my ability; it is the finest essence and the crowning decoration for the entire collection of sacred scriptures. || 2 || <note>The author suggests that astrology is the most vital "ornament" or accessory to the Vedas and other traditional sciences.</note>

This work, which always embodies the essence of all the sciences, was composed by Kalidasa to be pure, pleasing to the mind, and a source of delight for the learned. || 3 || <note>original: कालिदास (*Kālidāsa*). The text attributes itself to the most famous poet of classical Sanskrit literature. However, historians generally categorize this specific astronomical treatise as a later "pseudo-Kalidasa" work, likely from the 16th century, using the famous name to lend the text prestige.</note>

### Shri Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->Jammu<-

**No.** 846-Gha <note>original: ८४६- घ; ‘Gha’ is the fourth consonant of the Sanskrit alphabet, serving here as a shelf-mark or classification category.</note>

**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). In Sanskrit literary tradition, an ‘Abharanam’ (ornament or jewel) is a text that compiles the most polished and essential knowledge of a subject—in this case, the ‘Jyotirvida’ or the knowledge of one who understands the stars.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास; although attributed to the famous 5th-century classical poet Kalidasa, historians typically date this specific astrological treatise to a later period, possibly the 16th century, suggesting the author adopted the prestigious name to lend the work weight.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६; this indicates the total count of individual hand-written leaves, or folios, that comprise the manuscript.</note> **Age** ........................

**Subject** Astral Science <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (Jyotiṣam). This is the traditional Indian science of celestial bodies, which historically integrated mathematical astronomy, time-keeping, and astrological interpretation.</note>

# Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->Jammu<-

**No.** 846-Gha <note>original: ८४६-घ. The letter "Gha" is the fourth consonant of the Devanagari alphabet, used here as a shelf-mark or category indicator, similar to "Section D" in a modern filing system.</note>

**Title** <term>The Ornament of the Astrologer</term> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). A classic Sanskrit treatise on astrology and the calculation of auspicious times. The title suggests the knowledge within "adorns" or completes the expertise of a professional astrologer.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. Although it shares the name of the famous 4th-century poet, this scientific text is generally attributed by scholars to a later author (often called "Pseudo-Kalidasa") who used the name to provide the work with historical authority.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This figure represents the total number of individual folios (leaves) contained in this specific manuscript.</note> **Age** [not recorded]

**Subject** <term>Astral Science</term> <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (Jyotiṣam). In the traditional Indian context, this term refers to the "Science of Light," encompassing both mathematical astronomy and predictive astrology.</note>
</insert>

### Shree Raghunath Sanskrit Research Institute Library,
->Jammu<-

**No.** 846-Gha <note>original: ८४६-घ. The letter "Gha" is the fourth letter of the Devanagari alphabet, serving as a shelf-mark or classification category.</note>

**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). A well-known Sanskrit treatise on astrology and the calculation of auspicious moments (muhurta). The title implies that this knowledge serves as the "jewelry" or defining expertise of a learned astrologer.</note>

**Author** Kalidasa <note>original: कालिदास. Although the name is identical to the famous 4th-century poet, this scientific work is generally attributed to a later author (often referred to as "Pseudo-Kalidasa") who adopted the name to give the text greater prestige.</note>

**Extent** 356 <note>original: ३५६. This indicates the total number of individual folios, or leaves, contained in the manuscript.</note> **Age** [not recorded]

**Subject** Astral Science <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (Jyotiṣam). In traditional Indian education, this term encompasses the "Science of Light," which includes mathematical astronomy, the study of time, and predictive astrology.</note>
</insert>

->Jammu<-

**No.** <insert>846-Gha</insert> <note>original: ८४६- घ. The letter 'Gha' is the fourth letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a shelf-mark or classification code for the library’s organizational system.</note>

**Title** <insert>The Ornament of the Astrologer</insert> <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). A significant Sanskrit text on the science of auspicious time (muhurta) and astrology. The title poetically suggests that this knowledge is the "jewel" or crowning achievement of an expert practitioner.</note>

**Author** <insert>Kalidasa</insert> <note>original: कालिदास. While the text claims to be by the legendary 4th-5th century poet Kalidasa, historical analysis suggests it was composed by a later scholar using the famous name to lend the work authority.</note>

**Extent** <insert>356</insert> <note>original: ३५६. This denotes the total number of handwritten folios (leaves) contained within this specific volume.</note> **Age** ............................

**Subject** <insert>Astral Science</insert> <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (Jyotiṣam). This traditional field of study includes mathematical astronomy, the observation of celestial bodies, and the calculation of calendars and astrological charts.</note>

**Title** The Ornament of the Astrologer <note>original: ज्योतिर्विदाभरणम् (Jyotirvidābharaṇam). A foundational Sanskrit text concerning *muhurta* (auspicious timing) and mathematical astrology. **Subject** Astral Science <note>original: ज्योतिषम् (Jyotiṣam). This encompasses the traditional Indian study of celestial bodies, including both mathematical astronomy and astrology used for determining favorable times for rituals and life events.</note>
